Previous studies introduced the Sudakov-Fernique concentration inequality to address this issue by analyzing the efficiency of the optimized estimator in providing bounds on this distance. However, this inequality has a significant drawback, as it incorporates a non-decomposable term that hinders the application of the averaged marginally perturbed method (AMP) to demonstrate the correctness of the optimization procedure. In this paper, a new concentration inequality is derived that overcomes this limitation and provides a more flexible framework for studying the efficacy of optimization algorithms on complex landscapes. As a specific application, this paper demonstrates the validity of the TAP free energy for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model via the averaged marginally perturbed method (AMP). Which implies that the distance between the optimized value and the ideal statistic of interest can be bounded efficiently, and this inequality is sufficient to establish the correctness of the optimization procedure. In addition, this paper provides a combinatorial explanation for the efficiency of the optimized estimator, which is achieved by comparing the structure of the random graph defined by the optimized value with the model described by the Sudakov-Fernique metric. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through clustering of projection points, regardless of whether a 2D-2D correspondence problem is formulated to estimate pose in the second stage. This study introduces the concept of projection point clustering to demonstrate that CNN can generate a distribution of corresponding points on an object, thereby determining a 6D pose. The proposed pipeline demonstrates that clustering-based projection point distribution yields the most accurate results. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first determines the degree of variation between the node importance across different layers and then uses this information to calculate the eigenvector centrality values. We validate our method by demonstrating its applicability to a wide range of networks, including simple single-layer networks, complex single-layer networks, as well as real-world multi-layer networks. Our results show that network centrality values are influenced by the level of variation between different network layers and offer a suitable alternative to current multi-layer eigenvector centrality approaches. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. Our findings reveal that increased intermediate speeds accelerate pinch-off times, yet delay the start of the seal process; this speed range also exhibits varying splash dome closure rates. Our research includes statistical comparisons of water entry behaviors at different impact velocities to further understand these interactions. The reframing of our results in terms of flow acceleration offers new insights into the underlying mechanics, potentially leading to improved predictions of the surface seal process. The associated experimental and analytical methods involve high-speed camera recordings of water entry events, along with associated data analysis to derive precise velocity and time measurements. We also delve into the implications of these phenomena for various NLP applications and the difficulties they pose, such as establishing reliable evaluation metrics. Our study aims to contribute a comprehensive understanding of code-mixed NLP by interlocking the interconnected elements of language, technology, and society. We highlight specific research questions and possibilities for tackling difficult tasks like text classification and sentiment analysis. Our study also explores the ethical considerations involved in developing NLP models that incorporate encoded mixed languages and the challenges of scaling such models to large datasets that often include encoded mixed texts. We conclude by outlining future research directions, including developing customized NLP models for specific communities, creating high-quality annotated datasets for code-mixed data, and exploring techniques to transfer knowledge across different code-mixed languages. We explore the possibilities of using pre-trained multilingual models, the challenges of evaluating code-mixed NLP systems, and the risks of bias in NLP models that integrate encoded mixed languages. We also delve into the world of code-mixed generation, the challenges of developing customizable NLP models, and the challenges of scaling code-mixed NLP models to production. We conclude by outlining the challenges of developing NLP models that integrate encoded mixed languages, the risks of bias in these models, and the importance of transparency in NLP model interpretations. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target domain recommendation approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel concept, multi-sparse-domain (MSD) recommendation, which assumes multiple extremely sparse domains exist within the system. We then propose a novel MS-Domain recommendation framework, termed Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation via Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (MDCAPEAR), which leverages interactive content and rich user profiles to enhance aspect-specific preferences and domain-agnostic preference in a recursive manner. Notably, an innovative Dynamic Incentive Mechanism (DIM) is proposed to encourage users to engage fully in the system, providing valuable interactions that counteract data inflation. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MDCAPEAR over state-of-the-art baselines in various scenarios. Moreover, an in-depth analysis of the proposed framework, including theoretical proof of its stability and optimality, as well as the time and memory complexity of its implementation, is provided. The proposed approach as well as the theoretical analysis have been substantiated through realistic case studies. The code for MDCAPEAR is publicly available at https://github.com/tingting819/MDCAR.

The solution to a conic equation is a concept fundamental to convex optimization, defined as the smallest alpha value permitting the equation's left-hand side to be deemed feasible when scaled by a certain matrix. In the realm of real algebraic geometry, a similar notion exists, characterized as the smallest alpha value enabling the equation's solutions to comprise the entire space when scaled by the same matrix. Until now, researchers lacked access to a comprehensive theory for these solutions in algebraic geometry. This work establishes a connection between the two disciplines and demonstrates its practical application to a specific problem. Specifically, it shows that determining a conic equation's natural solution is equivalent to an optimization problem, with a specific objective function and matrix constraint. This analysis is further extended to the realm of bilinear equations, where it reveals an intrinsic relationship between the solution and the matrix's eigenvalues. A computational tool, Hypatia, is introduced, capable of efficiently computing these solutions for both conic and bilinear equations. In the process, it provides a set of algorithms that can be employed by other disciplines beyond algebraic geometry. The paper concludes with an examination of Hypatia's capabilities on a representative example drawn from convex optimization. The underlying code for these examples as well as additional documentation can be accessed via the paper's website. The development of Hypatia is ongoing and researchers are invited to contribute new ideas. The current version of Hypatia is tailored to work with Macaulay2, a free and open-source mathematical software system, and is compatible with Sage, another free and open-source mathematical software system. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an introductory overview of conic equations in the context of real algebraic geometry; Section 3 defines the solution to a conic equation and discusses its relationship with the matrix's eigenvalues; Section 4 introduces bilinear equations and the solution concept; Section 5 discusses the optimization-based interpretation of the solution concept for conic and bilinear equations; Section 6 examines the connection with convex optimization; and Section 7 presents an example drawn from convex optimization. The paper ends with an appendix containing the background material omitted from the main text. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. MRI data quality evaluation is a complex task that entails detecting and classifying various types of disturbances, artifacts, and image defects across different MRI protocols and modalities. This challenge is particularly pronounced in investigations involving lengthy, composite data collection processes like functional connectome mapping, as it demands continuous quality control measures to balance efficiency and overall study duration. This paper presents a novel approach to MRI data quality assessment, leveraging a combination of convolutional neural networks that accommodates multi-modal, multi-scan data analysis. This network's versatility enables effective generalization to unseen MRI protocols, scan parameters, and imaging modalities, all without additional training. The proposed method has been successfully applied to the evaluation of MRI data collected for functional connectome mapping, using 70 MRI scanners across three different modalities. The resulting code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub. This paper's findings have been published in previous studies, showing high accuracy in quality assessment and demonstrating the generalizability of the approach, as well as the effectiveness of MRI data quality assurance policies. The proposed method, combined with the associated code and research results, provide a valuable foundation for future advancements in MRI data quality assessment, protocol optimization, and data collection strategies. The code's accessibility enables researchers to explore generalization-based MRI data quality assessment and to analyze specific issues like artifact detection, as shown by an examination of an ECG-based MRI scenario. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the resilience of distribution networks, we developed a decision-making framework for optimal charging and driving paths utilizing a mix of short-term and long-term objectives. A two-layer optimization approach was implemented, featuring a dual-layer structure where micro-level decisions on charging and driving are made individually by vehicle owners, and these individual choices contribute to a higher-level, collective impact on the distribution network. A computational study was conducted in the context of a suburban area, incorporating real-world geography and transportation systems. It showed that the introduction of private EVs leads to an overload of the distribution network, possibly causing problems like phase separation, and that network infrastructure development is necessary to handle this issue. The study also found that, depending on pricing schemes and transportation options, private EV owners might charge their batteries during times of high load, exacerbating the problem of overloading, and that they tend to drive more frequently in areas served by different distribution networks, leading to phase separation, especially if there are physical barriers between these areas. The research was conducted in the United States, with results indicating that reducing load during peak charging hours could decrease the likelihood of overloading, and that implementing measures to discourage driving in different phases segments areas, thus reducing phase separation. The study concluded that private EVs exert significant pressure on distribution networks and urged policymakers to consider this impact when developing strategies to manage resilience in these networks. The research was funded by the National Science Foundation. The findings have been published in the IEEE Transactions on Power Systems journal. The code used in the study is available online, with a related video explaining the research available on YouTube. A review is given of the proposed models that incorporate extra quarks, such as the "little brother" of the top quark, which could explain the mass disparities between meson and baryon groups. Although these models predict an extremely heavy top-like quark to explain the data, alternative scenarios are also considered, such as particles made of conventional quarks with unusual charges, or those with extra quarks, as well as exotic mesons made of gluons, such as glueballs, mesons composed of four quarks (quadmesons), and mesons composed of two quarks and two antiquarks (hypermesons). The Coxeter group foundation theorem, initially proven by Bouscaren and Reutenauer, essentially states that a free group is generated by the elements of a Coxeter group if and only if the group's defining mirror reflections all possess infinite order. In this paper, we establish an analogous result for the basis elements of a exchange system associated with a finite irreducible quadratic diagram, specifically Diagram D of Nambu sense, following the format introduced by EiQi SuLi and YuGe Fu. Additionally, we investigate related properties and a significant result of Potocka's, concerning the group Sn(n+2) when n is an odd number greater than 1. Moreover, we establish an alternative proof of Potocka's result, as well as a related open problem. Lastly, we examine the foundation property of a specific class of groups, namely the biparabolic groups, and determine its connection to the Gelfand-Petrov metric. Lastly, we establish an analogue of the Coxeter group foundation theorem utilizing the Gelfand-Petrov metric. Lastly, we establish an analogue of the Coxeter group foundation theorem for the B-type Coxeter groups based on the basis elements of an exchange system associated with a finite irreducible diagram D of Nambu sense, specifically Diagram D of the sn(n+2) group when n is an odd number greater than 1.

The Pantheon SN Ia dataset can be combined with weak lensing observations to constrain the Hubble parameter and the matter density of the universe. The effect of lensing on SN Ia brightness is significant enough to be detected at a 7σ level, and this contribution correlates with SN Ia distance. By incorporating the redshift dependence of lensing, a model-independent approach is used to determine the lensing effect's impact on the SN Ia distance modulus. This analysis employs a new method that accounts for the redshift variation of lensing, which is caused by the changing effect of structure formation and its impact on both SN Ia distances and weak lensing. The result shows that the combination of SN Ia and weak lensing in the Pantheon sample is consistent with the standard model of cosmology, but there are signs of deviations from this model, particularly in the form of SN Ia lenses that are brighter than expected at higher redshifts. The standard model's breakdown at these redshift levels could be linked to the onset of dark energy's transition period. The predicted effect of lensing on SN Ia brightness in the Pantheon sample is also reflected in other datasets, including the SNLS3 and the Atlassian SN Ia datasets, which show similar patterns of deviation from the standard model. The nature of these deviations will be clarified by incorporating additional observations, particularly of the weak lensing shear in the specific skies corresponding to SN Ia locations. The predicted distributions of SN Ia lenses are also analyzed, which may vary significantly depending on specific models of galaxy evolution and the distribution of foreground and background objects. The predicted effect of lensing on SN Ia brightness will serve as a new standard marker for the standard model of the universe, which has been established based on the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and can be applied to other SN Ia datasets with similar characteristics. The predicted effect of lensing on SN Ia distances can be expressed as a constant shear of 0.15 mag, which is sufficient to explain the SN Ia lensing anomaly detected in some observations, and the predicted distributions of SN Ia lenses are consistent with the observed distributions of strong lensing in the Hubble Space Telescope images, which show that the vast majority of SN Ia lenses have magnifications of less than 0.5 mag and occur at distances of less than 2 billion light-years. Research on silicon material is expanding at a rapid pace to create efficient and miniaturized photonic devices. This study focuses on identifying and characterizing T defects in silicon material, specifically within the SOI platform. It demonstrates the distinctive features of T defects, including their unique absorption and emission spectra, and how they respond to various optical inputs. Furthermore, it shows that T defects can facilitate efficient forward-mode phase modulation and that they exhibit promising properties for uses such as quantum communication and quantum cryptography. It's also shown that T defects can exist in silicon materials grown using both melt-grown and solid-grown silicon on insulator materials, however they tend to reside at the interface between the silicon layer and the oxide layer. It's also demonstrated that T defects can be targeted and manipulated using a range of optical signals, including Raman, THz, and mid-IR light. It's also shown that T defects exhibit unique optical responses to their surrounding environments, however they can be sensitive to factors such as temperature, mechanical stress, and chemical exposure. It's also demonstrated that T defects can maintain their properties and stability even after being exposed to a range of optical signals and environmental conditions. The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a new form of the Moser's trace inequality for a domain that contains the origin, and a number of other key properties, we establish the existence and number of solutions to this system of equations for a specific range of the parameter $\varepsilon$ that is small enough. Additionally, we demonstrate the system's stability and the character of its solutions' variations with respect to the small parameter $\varepsilon$. Finally, we compare our results with those of existing research to demonstrate that our findings hold true in a broader context. The main objective of this research paper is to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that contains the origin and behaves like the Trudinger-Moser growth, as well as to provide a more detailed analysis of the system's solutions and the effects of the small parameter $\varepsilon$ on these solutions. The exact behavior of these variables is determined by the total number of groups $d$ and the number of independent variables $k$, leading to multiple cases such as $d=1$ (no correlation), $k=1$ (independent Bernoullies), and $d=k$ (Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution induced by inverse projections). For a binary random variable with zero mean, we apply the Varadhan-Sun method to obtain a large deviation principle, and using the Chernoff bound, we get inequality in the subcritical region. In the supercritical region, we obtain an exponential decay of expectation, and an upper bound on tail probabilities in the critical region. Additionally, we derive two moments bounds in the subcritical region, and the application in random permanent and Hamiltonian cycle problems is discussed. This paper introduces the concept of a symplectic transformation known as conversion, which transforms a given symplectic transformation into an equivalent form with a swapped role of variables and conjugate quantities. Conversion transformations have a straightforward representation as a matrix, which can be computed for a broad category of transformations. Specifically, a measure-preserving transformation has a matrix representation that consists of the inverse of its eigenvalue matrix. Additionally, the paper examines the relationship between conversion transformations and their associated topological properties, specifically its connection to its corresponding smooth differential equation. Furthermore, it provides a specific example of a measure-preserving transformation with two degrees of freedom, derived from a harmonic oscillator, which can be compared to a linear non-autonomous harmonic oscillator. The paper also explores the associated Melnikov function, the correlation function, and the diffusion coefficient for this specific example, as well as its associated standard mapping, which can be used to determine chaos through the standard criteria of the stroboscopic map. The results show that this specific example exhibits both chaotic behavior and stable periodic orbits, which can be found at both low-frequency random fluctuations and specific high-frequency periodic cases. The paper also highlights the importance of converting transformations in overcoming certain topological obstacles that prevent certain smooth differential equations from exhibiting chaotic behavior. The proposed approach provides a way to convert these types of equations into a more manageable form, which can be applied to a broad category of differential equations, including those with random fluctuations, periodic, or homogeneous turbulence. The paper also discusses its connection to Poincaré's question of whether a given differential equation can exhibit chaotic behavior, which is a significant open problem in mathematics. The proposed approach can be applied to demonstrate that at least a subset of the differential equations mentioned in the paper do exhibit chaotic behavior, which provides a way to answer Poincaré's question for this subset of differential equations. The results of the paper have been verified through numerical simulations, which are presented in the appendix. A key challenge in modern organ transplantation is managing kidney donations efficiently. Some patients wait indefinitely for a compatible organ, while healthy kidneys from registered donors go unused due to limited matching opportunities. To better understand this issue, we draw analogies from existing research in economics, specifically the optimal acceptance rules for donations or investments in a one-to-one matching market. By examining these patterns, we uncover suboptimal consequences of current allocation methods. For instance, a prominent priority-based allocation policy often results in poor performance. To overcome this, we suggest an alternative approach using Bayesian optimal acceptance rules. In a variety of scenarios, this method consistently delivers superior performance compared to priority-based policies. Furthermore, we find that the most recent research on Bayesian optimal acceptance rules, which utilizes complex, intricate methods, also yields comparable results when evaluating priority-based allocation. In the context of kidney transplants, our research suggests that hospitals should maintain detailed records of potential recipients's blood types to enhance allocation efficiency. Our study in a two-period model demonstrates that patients with rare blood types tend to wait longer for a compatible organ, while those with more common blood types receive a transplant more quickly. In a different scenario, where donations vary in quality, the outcome is similar, with patients possessing rare blood types experiencing better transplantation outcomes. On the other hand, patients with blood types considered ideal or too common may not benefit as much. Our research highlights the importance of a precise match between donor and recipient, even if it means transplating a kidney of higher quality at a lower frequency. In a different interpretation, where donations represent investments in a learning process, the outcome is similar, with patients possessing rare blood types experiencing better transplantation outcomes. In a different scenario, where donations vary in quality and patients can refuse up to half of the transplants, the outcome is also similar, with patients possessing rare blood types experiencing better transplantation outcomes. In a different scenario, where patients can choose between different organs from the same donor, the outcome is also similar, with patients possessing rare blood types experiencing better transplantation outcomes. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work also explores different model variants, places our findings within the broader context of thematic analysis, and examines the relationship between company names and the words that describe them. Our study suggests that word2vec embeddings reflect the complex structure of financial corpora, encompassing both co-occurring distributions and semantic meanings, thereby providing novel insights for the financial community. Our code is available at https://github.com/word-embedding-research-group.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based integrated data and energy transfer systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair throughfoy model parameters are assumed with $Fairness\_factor = 2.7$ and $Price\_per\_unit\_of\_energy = 0.01$.
In [1], the extra gain achieved with wideband waveforming was defined as the difference between the sum of data rate and harvested energy power and the product of the data rate and the fairness factor plus the product of the harvested energy power and the price per unit of energy.
We have also previously shown that wideband waveforming can result in significant gains, with values as high as 1000 times more advantageous than using any single subcarrier.
Our results demonstrate notably small disparities between the optimal SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM solutions, as well as between the optimal and the two-tier SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM solutions.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've compared our results to established literature, demonstrating close agreement and improving the resolution of certain scenarios. To accommodate dynamic boundary conditions, we've introduced a numerical predictor--corrector technique and implemented a simple algorithm for efficient level-set reinitialization, both of which are crucial components of our model. In multiagent systems, an equilibrium is a stable state where agents' actions do not change, reflecting a balance of interests and potential countermeasures. However, the complexity of the underlying system often renders equilibria difficult to understand and analyze for individual agents or external observers. In response to this challenge, we develop a general framework for learning explainable equilibria in multiagent systems. Within this framework, an external observer can express the environment as a Markov decision process, attribute states to action profiles, and infer the behavior of agents based on observed actions. Given this perspective, we demonstrate that an external observer can determine whether an action profile is an equilibrium and, in addition, obtain a compact summary of the underlying system that corresponds to the equilibrium action profile. In the process, our method also identifies whether the environment is complex or simple. If the environment is simple, we further demonstrate that an external observer can learn the action profile that corresponds to a given performance metric over time. In the course of our analysis, we propose a novel approach that combines the concept of a discarding function from the theory of Markov decision processes with the concept of a projective cover from the theory of algebraic geometry. This approach yields a generalizable algorithm for solving complex systems, as well as a theoretical bound on complexity for solo agents. We support our findings with simulation experiments in multiagent systems and compare our method against multiple baselines, in addition to providing code available online. In addition, we apply our method to a real-world socioeconomical system, the GDP of countries during the Cold War era. In this case, our method accurately reconstructs the underlying structure of the system, correctly predicts the actions of individual countries, and leverages graph neural networks to learn this structure. We term this generalizable model the Explainable Equilibrium Learning Through Graph Unrolling framework, in addition to providing code available online. The model involves an undirected graph whose edges change at unknown rates, and the epidemic spreads at a rate proportional to the product of the densities of infected individuals in the surrounding neighborhood and a measure of the graph's accessibility at each node. The main focus is on examining the long-term behavior of the epidemic, with particular emphasis on determining the epidemic's duration's distribution when the edge change rates can be categorized into two levels: supercritical and critical. The research also explores the concept of a threshold between the epidemic's endemic and outbreak phases. Integrating datasets from various sources, including flux measurements, deep inelastic scattering data, and saturation data, necessitates a theoretical foundation that connects parton distribution functions, structure functions, and scattering processes. This connection can be complex due to the diverse nature of datasets, requiring a conversion between different processes and reactions. A key challenge is addressing the different scales used in processes and reactions, such as deep inelastic scattering, hadron colliders, and heavy ion collisions, which involve processes like scattering off protons or heavy ions, and involve neutral or charged bosons. A new framework is proposed to provide a unified approach to PDF fitting, effectively handling datasets from various sources, incorporating recent advancements in QCD and saturation theory, and ensuring consistency across different scales, orientations, and processes. This proposed framework can be applied to fit parton distribution functions using a range of processes and reactions, and it is suitable for experiments like the Electron-Ion Collider, the Future Circular electron-positron Collider, and the Large Hadron Collider. Although developed with the needs of the Electron-Ion Collider in mind, this framework can also be utilized by other experiments, such as the Large Hadron Collider at higher energies, with some modifications. A comprehensive investigation into the proposed framework's capabilities is conducted, including comparative analyses with existing methods, evaluations of constraints on parton distribution functions, and studies of intrinsic charm quarks. A unique feature of this framework is the inclusion of intrinsic charm quark components within parton distribution functions, which it demonstrates can be an essential element in parton distribution functions, especially for certain processes and reactions. A note is made about the relationship between parameters used in processes and reactions, which can be converted into each other, and the proposed framework provides theoretical support for these conversions. A key challenge addressed by this framework is the discrepancy between parton distribution functions determined using different processes and reactions, which it demonstrates can be resolved by considering intrinsic charm quark components and orientation effects within parton distribution functions. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework's capabilities is presented, which includes applications to processes and reactions, conversions between process and reaction parameters, and comparisons with experimental data, all of which support the effectiveness of this framework in connecting processes and reactions, and providing consistent parton distribution functions. A call is made for experiments to prioritize processes and reactions that can determine orientation effects and intrinsic charm quark components within parton distribution functions, which will greatly enhance the accuracy and capabilities of parton distribution functions. To enhance the effectiveness of experience replay in addressing conceptual challenges resembling distribution drift and preference for early trials, we introduce a new approach that modifies the variance of a sample batch by either increasing the significance of less successful experiences or the impact of more successful ones, depending on the phase of learning. We analyze this method's impact to demonstrate its potential to mitigate experience decay and facilitate smoother policy updates. Experimentally, our findings indicate that for a significant number of difficult tests, varying the variance of a sample batch can lead to performance improvements for state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. We also discover that the best approach varies based on the specific challenge the model is attempting to overcome. In general, minimizing the variance of a sample batch is consistently found to be beneficial. Our proposed method proves particularly effective when there are substantial discrepancies within the data distribution, leading to difficulties in model generalization. We demonstrate this in a challenging navigation scenario that requires modeling multiple diverse environments. In addition to this, we identify several possible future enhancements to further boost the already effective method of varying the variance of a sample batch. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ShuaiNg/VDER.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our approach to this problem combines 
multiple text generation models through weighted blending, allowing for diverse 
output in response to varying listener types. Our findings on various evaluation 
metrics reveal consistent performance improvements achieved through multi-branch 
evaluation and consideration of listener types, resulting in a 19 percentage 
point improvement in accurate branch prediction. Our research, alongside the vast 
MultiTalk Dataset, is available at https://yilundu.github.io/multalk/.

We introduce a method for creating modified gravity simulations in the context of cosmological scales, with the aim of differentiating similar gravity theories, such as f(R) theories, with up-to-date observational data. This approach leverages the insight that the metric convergence induced by massive structures is sensitive to the underlying theory of gravity. A key aspect of this method is the utilization of reduced simulation data, specifically the cross-correlation of gravitational fields, which serves as a key predictor for modified gravity theories. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we employed a novel multi-resolution grid technique to perform full N-body simulations in a controlled environment, and then applied a machine learning model to predict the effects of modified gravity on dark matter distributions in the Coma cluster. The results highlight the capability of machine learning algorithms in predicting the effects of modified gravity on individual galaxies, and the relevance of simulation data over simplified analytic models. Ultimately, this research provides a framework for using N-body simulations to explore the differences between various gravity theories, and a practical example of using machine learning on the Coma cluster. The simulation data and software used in this study are available for public access. The current state of the project offers numerous opportunities for further development and refinement. A key idea in the study of the Gaussian free field (GFF) in relation to stochastic loop erased walks (SLE) lies in designing a combined model. Specifically, a unit GFF is paired with multiple independent SLEs, whose intersection angles add up to $2\pi$. The behavior of these combined models is understood when multiple SLEs share a common boundary component, particularly in regards to their boundary component(s) and interior branches. Our research reveals that the combined model consists of multiple separate SLEs evolving in a complex plane filled with an independent Poisson point process of Macdonald functions along the real axis. Conversely, we can also obtain the Gaussian free field derived from the combined model. Notably, the chordal version of this scenario is also established. Our results can be realized through an explicit construction of the combined model, thereby providing an alternative explanation of its behavior. Furthermore, our findings may be viewed as a version of the Radon-Nikodym theorem for measures, which can be extended to a broader context involving measures driven by random log-gases. The transition from a single SLE to a many-skeleton SLE also arises as a specialized case from our combined model. The statistics of local geometries, particularly branch points and boundary angles, are also calculated in our results. These calculations are significant because they demonstrate that the combined model is infinitely divisible, thereby extending the meaning of this term beyond its common limitation to the domain marking tree. The measure-driven SLE perspective of our results may also be viewed as a means of implementing the idea of infinite divisibility in the context of a domain marked tree. The many-skeleton SLE scenario can be realized through a simple and explicit construction, which may be stochastic or deterministic. In the latter case, an explicit formula for a related measure-driven SLE has been derived. This formula may be useful for testing many SLE approximation algorithms, particularly those involving the Schramm-Loewner evolution in a domain with multiple boundary components. The change from a single SLE to a many-skeleton SLE also arises from our combined model when the point process consisting of Macdonald functions along the real axis is replaced by a point process defined within a finite domain. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source version of the Wikipedia infrastructure, allowing for private and customizable knowledge-sharing environments. Originally developed in 2008 by the Monod Lab, this version of MediaWiki has been utilized by multiple research groups across the globe. It incorporates features such as tailored permissions, a distinct repository for data and scripts, and sophisticated collaboration tools. We present WorkingWiki Version 1.7, incorporating key advancements and proposed improvements, in the form of a technical guide for developers and potential users. By sharing this version, we aim to provide a starting point for creating tailored Wiki applications and to foster collaboration and knowledge exchange among developers working on private MediaWiki instances. The source code for WorkingWiki 1.7 is available at https://github.com/WorkingWiki/WorkingWiki. Version 1.7's derivation from the core MediaWiki 1.32.1, along with installation and configuration instructions, can be found at the aforementioned GitHub link.

The LHC is an versatile accelerator that can produce a wide range of secondary particles, both through nucleon-nucleus collisions and with various beam combinations. This paper overviews the achievements and potential of LHC facilities for conducting deep minor system research, focusing on experiments that utilize the MIRO detector at the CERN Beam Test Facility, the ALICE and LHCb detectors at the CERN Interaction Point, and the SHARK detector at the LHCb long straight pipe. Despite the diverse sites and setups, a unified approach is employed to analyze data, leveraging advanced software tools that enable combination of individual detectors' outputs, tracking, and event selection. This has led to notable discoveries, including the identification of antiproton fragments, which were previously unknown, and the study of antihelicity polarization in certain reactions. As the LHC continues to operate and new facilities are developed, there are significant opportunities ahead, including optimization of detectors, exploration of new beams and collision configurations, and integration with other experiments, which are expected to yield even more breakthroughs in minor system research. This work is part of the LHC Physics with Test Beams workshop series, and involves collaboration with the LHC Physics with Antiprotons workshop series. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring patterns of behavior. This study challenges that idea by revealing that the intervals between which neutron star binaries experience outbursts are not random and can be explained by a single distribution that applies across the sample, whether it includes the suspected black hole binaries or not. When taking into consideration the time it takes for these sources to experience outbursts, the difference between the groups becomes even more distinct, suggesting that the sources that have shown no outbursts in the observed time frame are actually neutron star binaries rather than black holes. This finding can be further confirmed by the fact that the outburst intervals of the suspected black hole binaries align with the period of the Milky Way. This distribution of outburst intervals also offers a potential explanation for the sources that have shown no outbursts in the observed time frame, indicating that some of these sources may have experienced an outburst recently but have not been monitored adequately. The study utilized a comprehensive database of known neutron star binary systems within the Milky Way, incorporating sources that have experienced outbursts in the X-ray and optical spectrums. The analysis covered approximately 24 sources, including the suspected black hole binaries at the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade, such as AX J174417-36146, 2XMMi J180103.8-245249, 1RXS J162753-495148, 1RXH J162754.9-495149, 2XMMi J173808.8-350850, and GX 339-4 (also known as V411 Persei). The research relied on the King-Altman generator function, the Weibull distribution, and the generalized inverse Gaussian function to model the distribution of outburst intervals. The results showed that the sources that have shown no outbursts in the observed time frame experience outbursts more frequently than the sources that have experienced outbursts in the observed time frame, with the former having a distribution of outburst intervals less than 10 years. Understanding the meaning of conversations relies heavily on grasping the semantics of individual words and phrases, as well as their combined semantic variety within the conversation. While evaluating word and phrase semantics has traditional assessments, there's no established method to measure the semantic variety of conversations, which is crucial for evaluating the performance of dialogue systems in an inference-based framework. We introduce a novel approach to assess the semantic variety of conversations by utilizing Natural Language Inference tasks, which can be applied at both the sentence and paragraph levels. We also design a dedicated task, Semantic Variety in Dialogue, where the objective for dialogue systems is to produce conversations with optimal semantic variety relative to a reference paragraph, as evaluated by human assessors and automated NLI-based metrics. Our findings with a sample dataset demonstrate that evaluating word and phrase semantics is insufficient and that evaluating the semantic variety of conversations is crucial for developing more intelligent dialogue systems. Our research is accessible through an interactive notebook presenting basic concepts, evaluation methods, and algorithmic implementations to produce dialogue systems for the Semantic Variety in Dialogue task. We anticipate this work will inspire researchers to explore the complex issue of semantic variety in conversations. We have made our code available at https://github.com/nyu-dl4mt/cse6024_svd.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. The simulation of the second scenario revealed a critical point where further mass loss no longer shrinks the star, allowing it to reach a stable equilibrium with a rocky core. The occurrence of this point varied based on angular momentum, rather than mass. The simulation also considered the effects of mass loss and spin on the star's surface temperature, showing that it remains relatively constant, and allowed the estimation of angular momentum required for stable equilibrium. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an iterative procedure for discovering such a representation, with an analysis of its properties leading to a parameterized algorithm solving the issue in time proportional to the number of nodes to a certain exponent. The method has further value as a preprocessing step to enhance the accuracy of existing edge-reduction methods, the layout algorithms Target Edge Length and Multi-Column Cross Minimization specifically. The paper concludes by outlining outstanding challenges in optimizing the current approach, particularly the identification of more efficient search patterns to reduce the number of node split operations required. The proposed method has been implemented and is available as a part of the GraphDrawing library for the Java programming language. The paper presents theoretical and experimental results validating the approach's effectiveness and analyzing the relationship between the input graph characteristics and the procedure's performance. The paper's findings are further illustrated using a real-world dataset. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking using thrusters with separate power and torque inputs, which results in a more efficient and robust gait. By considering the negative effects of certain thrusting movements, our model incorporates constraints to limit counterproductive actions. Unlike previous models, the proposed algorithm accounts for varied terrain conditions and threatens a better grip on the ground by positioning the center of mass within a secure boundary. Utilizing a simulation platform with validated results, we demonstrate the benefits of thruster-supported locomotion in real-world scenarios. Compared to conventional actuation systems, our proposed design achieves a 25% decrease in average power consumption and a 50% drop in the maximum displacement of the center of mass during movement. Moreover, by incorporating redundancy into the model, researchers are given the opportunity to explore various co-screw transformations that could lead to new insights into biomimicry. The code for the simulations is available online at https://github.com/thruster-robotics/thruster-locust.

We've demonstrated that a specific knot invariant, arising from a modification of the Fox-Hatcher loop, possesses a particular property - it can be categorized within the most advanced Vassiliev invariant category of order three. This achievement builds on a previous discovery by the second listed author, proving that the original Fox-Hatcher loop defines a Vassiliev invariant of the second order. A straightforward expansion of the Fox-Hatcher loop for a particular type of linked knots enables the creation of a new invariant, which can be represented through a specific combinatorial object called a decorated stitch. This decorated stitch representation facilitates the development of the mentioned order three Vassiliev invariant, by employing a decomposition approach similar to that introduced by the second listed author. A more intricate analysis of the decorated stitches also allows us to define an invariant for embedded curves, which can be utilized to demonstrate that the mentioned order three Vassiliev invariant is inherently intrinsic and cannot be expressed through lower order Vassiliev invariants. A related investigation into the properties of the embedded curve invariant also yields results on the behavior of this invariant under specific curve modifications, which may be of independent interest. A comparable version of the order three Vassiliev invariant is shown to arise from a change in the base used for the Fox-Hatcher loop, which implies that this version is also intrinsic and coincides with the previously defined version. Finally, we established a relationship between the order three Vassiliev invariant and the composite of the József Kökl's invariant and the branching number, which can be expressed through the combinatorial object of the decorated stitch. This paper delves into the realm of federated learning that is characterized by a horizontal data exchange pattern among participants. We have derived two distinct privacy-exploiting tactics, referred to as "Privacy-Assaulting Machine Learning Attacks," aimed at compromising a server in a federated learning environment. The first attack, known as "Lieu", targets model training by manipulating data to deceive the server into revealing sensitive information about a particular individual. The second attack, known as "Copy", focuses on data analysis by infiltrating a model to extract private information from a subset of participants. We have further investigated the conditions under which these attacks are successful and provided two different options for executing them: one is straightforward and the other is more intricate but more effective. We have also developed an algorithm to determine the optimal attack duration and another to validate the effectiveness of the attacks in various settings. The results of our experiments reveal that both attacks are highly practical and capable of unveiling sensitive information from a server in a federated learning environment with horizontal data transfer, even when implemented under strict privacy constraints. We have further compared our attacks to other privacy-threatening tactics and demonstrated that they are both highly effective in revealing information about individuals. Finally, we have discussed the implications of our findings and proposed potential strategies for enhancing the security of federated learning environments. We have made our code available to the public for review. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel estimation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both a randomized and low-dimensional feature space transformation. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. In all evaluations, our method yields superior performance in terms of both efficiency and accuracy. In particular, we find that our method excels at handling difficult linearly non-separable problems, as well as those involving high-dimensional input variables, and further analyze the theoretical guarantees of our method, demonstrating its connection to the concept of the kernel matrix's intrinsic dimension, a novel idea introduced in this paper. In addition, we make publicly available our code for our method, named DeepFF, on GitHub. In order to demonstrate its practical applicability, we successfully apply DeepFF to the task of linearly supporting non-linearly classifyable MRI images, a challenging problem of significant clinical interest. In all, our results validate the premise that kernel methods based on randomized features can become unnecessarily complex when dealing with small sample sizes, and that there are better, more efficient alternatives available. In contrast, on the other hand, we find that RFF is capable of handling larger datasets, and that both RFF and our method can efficiently handle linearly separable problems. In all, our method offers a novel perspective on the concept of the kernel matrix's intrinsic dimension, a measure that can be utilized to evaluate the efficacy of both existing and novel kernel-based methods. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We have obtained two primary results regarding these hypersurfaces. Firstly, under the assumption that one of these hypersurfaces has a non-zero mean curvature, we have proven that it must be isotopic to a sphere with a specific radius, subject to a particular symmetry. Secondly, we have discovered that there are only three possible topological classifications for hypersurfaces with zero mean curvature in this specific space setting. Additionally, we have established that these positively curved hypersurfaces are rigorously classified as topological spaces. This latter conclusion can be seen as a extension of the renowned M\"obius scalar curvature flexibility theorem. The research paper also reviews previous work by other mathematicians, whose contributions are presented in the initial sections. The paper's main findings are presented in the results section, with the final section outlining potential future research and the approach used to achieve the findings presented in the results section. The paper also includes an appendix, containing a key integration result and a topological hypersurface classification theorem. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single edge in a Cayley tree network. Specifically, they investigate the impact on the network's connectivity and identify a key threshold below which the removal of a single edge leads to a massive cascade effect, resulting in the network's splitting into isolated components. The authors also determine the probability distribution of the magnitude of these cascade effects. The proposed approach can be applied to general random networks and may serve as a foundation for more broad-based measures of network vulnerability. Furthermore, this research provides a pure theoretical analysis, which may be of interest to mathematical researchers. However, these properties are still partially unknown, especially in the high-density region of neutrons. A statistical model, the Relativistic Mean Field model, was applied to the "Big Apple" region, which refers to the area on the neutron-star-mass versus spin-rate plot indicating the most susceptible region to effects caused by neutron instability and oscillations. By adjusting the parameters of the model, we evaluated the "Big Apple" region's properties to predict patterns of neutron-star behavior in binary neutron star mergers. Furthermore, we explored the possible influence of the "Big Apple" region on astrophysical objects, including binary neutron star mergers, neutron stars with soft gamma-ray bursts, and supernovas that produced neutron star remnants. We found that the "Big Apple" region exhibits distinct characteristics that could be identified by measuring the angular momenta of low-mass neutron-star binaries formed in the remnants of binary neutron star mergers. Additionally, we found that the "Big Apple" region's effects on the behavior of these binaries are likely to be minimal, with an estimated frequency of less than 10% for the most susceptible objects, including R Corbori and RE J0513+413. However, the "Big Apple" region could influence the behavior of the HESS J0731+495 high-energy pulsar electron stream, and the characteristics of the K2 1048+353 neutron-star binary. We also proposed a method for measuring the "Big Apple" region's properties by analyzing the angular momenta of low-mass neutron-star binaries formed in the remnants of binary neutron star mergers. We estimated that this method is capable of detecting a specific property of the "Big Apple" region that indicates neutron-star behavior caused by instability and oscillations, and which could influence the interpretation of future data from gravitational wave detectors, such as LIGO and VIRGO, and X-ray telescopes, such as the X-ray Telescope. This research focuses on creating precise, long-lasting Molmer-Sorensen gates using ion trapped systems, taking advantage of multiple motional modes to enhance frequency stability and expand beyond the reach of a single mode. A frequency-stable gate generation mechanism based on balanced signal generation across multiple modes is developed and analyzed, demonstrating through numerical simulations that it can achieve high levels of frequency stability and duration expandability. Specifically, calculations show that with two modes, the gate's frequency stability can be made at least ten times more precise, and its duration can be extended by several times relative to using a single mode. Furthermore, investigating a system with three modes, researchers found that placing a motional mode in a Lambdberg regime to minimize frequency drift significantly improves the gate's frequency stability and duration, making it possible to achieve precise control over 10 motional modes. The proposed gate generation mechanism, utilizing balanced signal generation across multiple modes, offers a versatile approach for addressing a wide range of motion levels, and the research findings are relevant to various trapped ion systems. The code used in this research has been made available online, allowing for replication of the results and exploration of other trapped ion systems. The chapter also concludes by outlining potential pathways for further improvement, including the use of optimized balancing signals, multi-level configurations, and surface trapped ions, as well as the connections to related research topics, such as quantum simulation and error correction. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with certain modifications. We discovered that a heavily reduced neural model performs on par with the full model in several assessments. Building upon this discovery, we developed a method where a neural model's residual is learned in relation to an $n$-gram model to create a more efficient and streamlined neural model. When applied to text summarization and generation, this model delivered outstanding results, outperforming the conventional BART model in various evaluation metrics. Notably, it also achieved notable improvements when used for low-resource scenarios. The code and models are available at GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves simple and broad generalization, demonstrating superior results on more challenging datasets such as the recently launched AFLW2019-3D. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghristian/SADRNet.

However, in models with a monodromy, this outcome is hindered by the field's nature and its potential. This outcome holds for all scales, as the formation of black holes is determined by the disturbance in the gradient of the scalar field rather than its absolute value. This particular scenario can also occur in other inflationary models, as it primarily depends on the structure of the potential. A key factor for integrating renewable energy sources into the grid is effective storage systems. To understand the potential of different storage technologies, we examine self-allocation strategies for household storage units in decentralized markets. Current models typically assume that individuals act rationally and maximize their economic gains. However, our research considers the implications of consumers being risk-averse, which could make household storage less appealing. By utilizing a recent approach from risk-averse individualization, we show that decentralized markets can be modeled using a suitable equivalent problem, which allows us to focus on a representative agent that is rational and risk-averse. This enables us to analyze storage adoption using a simple metric and explores the interplay between storage costs, risk, and electricity prices. Interestingly, we find that risking some income on the market can make storage a more attractive option, which may surprise some experts. Additionally, our findings suggest that the risk associated with market prices has a more significant impact on storage adoption than the risk associated with storage degradation. This, along with other insights, can be obtained by mapping the self-allocation problem to a stochastic stop-the-losse problem. Our research can be applied to various household storage units, such as thermal energy storage systems, biomass storage systems, hydro energy storage systems, and chemical energy storage systems, including batteries, which are effective in reducing renewable energy curtailment. If consumers become less risk-averse, our results show that storage adoption increases, although the relationship between storage adoption and risk is more complex. On the other hand, if the cost of storage decreases, our analysis indicates that storage adoption increases for both risk-averse and risk-neutral consumers. Moreover, our findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between the risks associated with market prices and storage degradation, which can be applied to appropriate storage technologies, such as batteries that have minimal degradation risk. Our research provides a platform for exploring other storage technologies, such as liquefied air energy storage systems, sodium-ion battery systems, zinc-air battery systems, and metal-air battery systems, which can further reduce renewable energy curtailment. Our proposed "dynamic learning" technique tackles issues related to large-scale neural network training, specifically focusing on the challenges of efficient data preprocessing and optimal model updating. We show that by utilizing a separate neural network to identify and target specific data classes, we can significantly enhance the effectiveness of our dynamic learning approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this technique can be applied to various tasks, including classification, regression, and anomaly detection, and even enable seamless model updates without knowing the exact distribution of the new data. We have tested "dynamic learning" on several benchmarks and real-world scenarios and have found it to be highly successful. Our code is now available on GitHub at the specified URL. As artificial intelligence technology advances and Machine Learning models gain significant popularity, trust in their accuracy and reliability is expected to rise. However, several issues related to data quality, model limitations and security concerns hinder a full-scale integration. We propose a collaborative agent framework that addresses these obstacles by incorporating a duo of expert agents. The first agent, responsible for quality assessment, identifies and rectifies inconsistent data. The second agent, dedicated to model enhancement, suggests possible improvements to a questionable model by presenting potential data augmentations. Both agents present their suggestions in the form of trust scores to the system, which are then combined to determine the level of trust placed in the model. This trust level is displayed to the user along with the proposed data augmentation. If the level of trust is insufficient, the user has the option to either validate the data, validate the model enhancement suggestion, or ignore the advice. In doing so, the user generates a rich set of outcomes that can be used to update the model and enhance its performance. Through simulation studies, the proposed framework demonstrates its capability to learn from user input and correct model errors, ultimately leading to a more reliable and adaptable Machine Learning model. The system's flexibility is further highlighted by the ease with which new features can be integrated into the system. The potential of this framework for real-world applications is significant, with possibilities in industries related to self-driving technology, finance and medical research. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT, have led to significant gains in WSD accuracy by employing a zero-shot or few-shot learning approach.  However, these successes primarily focus on leveraging general language properties without accounting for the specific semantic details included in gloss context.  Our investigation reveals that gloss context is frequently overlooked, with many top-performing models performing below 50% accuracy in certain cases.  We propose a simple yet effective strategy, context-gloss augmentation, to enhance the efficacy of BERT-based WSD models by incorporating gloss context in a way that prevents semantic drift.  Our evaluation shows that simply integrating this approach into existing few-shot methods leads to a substantial improvement in performance, with an average 12% accuracy gain across the Senseval datasets.  Interestingly, our analysis uncovers instances where the gap between context-gloss averages a 30% accuracy difference, highlighting the significance of gloss context in certain scenarios.  Ultimately, our context-gloss augmentation is a versatile technique with widespread applications, including both zero-shot and semi-supervised WSD settings.  We demonstrate its effectiveness in these scenarios, achieving an additional 5-7% accuracy gain.  With its simplicity and versatility, our context-gloss augmentation is a valuable addition to the WSD toolkit, presenting a promising direction for future research by encouraging the community to explore the underlying issues causing gloss context to be overlooked in certain cases.  We also release our code and a detailed analysis of the dataset at https://github.com/ContextGloss/Word-Sense-Disambiguation.

This study forms the basis of a comprehensive exploration. It introduces a set of integral definitions for the reciprocal gamma function, which includes a formal introduction of the regularized gamma function and several of its variations, including a generalized and an extended version of the 1940 Watson's formula. Furthermore, established and novel integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function are examined, and new expressions derived from hypergeometric functions are presented. Additionally, this study shows that the regularized gamma function can be expressed as the coefficient of a term in a series expansion, and obtains a general integral representation of this function. Lastly, this research provides a specific example of an integral representation of the reciprocal gamma function and establishes its connection to the hypergeometric function based on a specific integral representation of the regularized beta function. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL understanding, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance filling values, we introduce a column selection task to facilitate filling values, and for schema linking, we adopt a strategy combining explicit links with default mappings. Experiments using the Spider dataset demonstrate that incorporating column selection improves the performance of value filling, while strategic linking selection based on natural language cues in statements about unknown columns proves effective in areas with limited explicit links. Furthermore, our findings indicate performance enhancements in filling values and accurate schema linking in areas with sufficient explicit links. We propose a simple yet effective approach to make default mappings more precise and demonstrate that incorporating auxiliary tasks, specifically column selection with a flat schema, simplifies schema linking to match the difficulty of other Spider tasks. Our approach achieves the best results across all sections of the Spider dataset according to various evaluation metrics. Additionally, we show that nearly 70% of statements about unknown columns are accurate, and our approach successfully predicts the schema columns targeted in statements about unknown columns with an F1 score of 0.57. Our code is available at github.com/zwang93/TextToSQLAuxiliary.

This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in differential privacy applications, with a focus on network-structured data. We define a new concept of a reducing surface within a metric space that contains two separate regions divided by a surface with finite area, and is equipped with a specific mapping property in a specific homotopy class. This type of surface is then used to create a minimization problem, and its solution is dubbed a regional minimizing surface. We establish criteria for a surface to be considered regional minimizing, and also demonstrate the existence of a surface that is both regional minimizing and area-minimizing in certain situations where the metric space has certain properties. Additionally, we find that in the absence of topological restrictions, regional minimizing surfaces can map continuously to any surface within the same homotopy class. If the metric space is compact and surfaces are defined by Cartan's division property, then we prove that being regional minimizing and area-minimizing are equivalent properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that region-minimizing surfaces are akin to vascular surfaces, and that any surface that is both regional minimizing and area-minimizing can be modified to become vascular. If the metric space is compact and surfaces are defined by Cartan's division property, then we show that it is possible to remove the topological restriction from region-minimizing surfaces that are also area-minimizing by utilizing a blow-up technique near singular points.
