Creating realistic virtual injuries for human heads is a challenging task that requires significant artistic experience and technical expertise. Traditional approaches rely heavily on human input, while machine learning methods can automate the process, but current models struggle with creating diverse, realistic injuries that resemble real-world data. To address this limitation, we introduce a innovative framework called BRAIN (Brain Injury Generation Network), a three-layer, variational adversarial network that produces varied, realistic injuries on brain images. Specifically, it uses a latent space to control the presence, type, and location of injuries, while a classification network determines the type and a regression network indicates the level of damage. To ensure diversity and realism, BRAIN incorporates a progressive strategy and a multi-scale discriminator. Evaluations using custom datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of BRAIN in generating diverse, realistic injuries on brain images. Furthermore, we show that BRAIN can be applied in a secondary task, such as injury-level classification, following the success of the main task, to improve performance. Compared to baseline methods, BRAIN significantly improves performance in various evaluation metrics. The code for BRAIN is available at https://github.com{:/steps/Brain-Injury-Generation Network}. To demonstrate the versatility of BRAIN, we create a simulation scenario where it generates realistic injuries on realistic head models used in automotive safety testing. The code for this simulation is available at https://github.com{:/steps/Head-Injury-Simulation}. The findings of this study have important implications for the use of machine learning models in automotive safety testing and related applications. The research has been conducted by the steps research group at the Singapore University of Technology and Architecture under the ADAS project funded by the Singapore government. The project aims to advance safety mobility through the development of safe and innovative vehicular technologies. The findings of this research have significant technological and practical value in several areas including automotive safety testing, video game development, and medical education. The code for BRAIN has been successfully applied in these areas, in addition to brain injury synthesis, by generating realistic injuries on brain images for use in educational and research purposes. The code for Head-Injury-Simulation has been used to create realistic head models with injuries in automotive safety testing and has been successfully applied in several scenarios including in video game development, medical education, and biomechanical modeling. The research has also identified several open issues including but not limited to, the use of transfer learning for brain injury classification, the development of robust adversarial networks for brain injury generation, and the creation of large datasets for brain injury analysis.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the development process for programs utilizing rooted rules, the GP 2 compiler has been enhanced to include a new rule learning technique. This method enables the automatic creation of rooted rules from existing program code, facilitating quick matching and thus a significant reduction in program execution time. Moreover, the EPGP toolset has been developed to support this process, comprising a validator, a rule learning tool, and a command-line interface for demonstrating the proposed concept. The underlying principle of the root rule learning technique has further implications for the theory of graph translation, contributing a new approach to defining graph translation functions. Additionally, this approach enables the distinction between distinct translation properties, as well as the identification of the precise property that defines the image of a given graph translation. The research into root rule learning has also uncovered a learned rule's intrinsic property, termed the inheritance property. This property enables efficient matching of pre-existing rules against programs generated from initial conditions, further extending the GP 2 framework's capabilities. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. Nonetheless, a persistent and formerly reported issue arises in the form of a slow-sided hot plate phenomenon, thus far unaddressed in the literature. Despite this shortcoming, this model has been successfully applied to various variation scenarios including rotating, horizontal layer, and turbulent Rayleigh-Benard convection, in addition to atmospheric convection within a very basic single-column model. These results demonstrate that even a straightforward two-fluid model can capture the underlying dynamics of these scenarios, setting the stage for further enhancement and subsequent application to more complex three-dimensional variations. Moreover, the issue of the slow-sided hot plate phenomenon remains an ongoing challenge that requires urgent attention from the computational dynamics community. The associated code for this project is available at https://github.com/MarkHawkins-RayBenard. The dynamics underlying the mentioned scenarios are predominantly influenced by the interface between converging and descending fluid elements, thus differing significantly from the assumptions of traditional linear stability analysis, which predicts that these elements become evenly distributed following convection onset. Nonetheless, even in the presence of forced asymmetry, the accumulation of ascending elements in the upper region and the convergence of descending elements in the lower region remains evident, thereby validating the two-fluid model. The association between the heat transfer and the convection driven force remains nonlinear in relation to the Rayleigh number, yet shares a resemblance with the renowned $Ra^{1/3}$ relationship, the underlying cause of which has been determined to be related to the sudden onset of side wall heat and mass transfer exchange in this particular scenario. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to determine under what conditions this unconnected system can still be entangled with the other two. Our results show that if the unconnected system's cavity has a strong enough resonance with its own two-photon state, it is possible to create a sincere Bell state among the three atoms. This achievement is observed in simulations, which demonstrate that both genuine tripartite entanglement and sine-squared correlation properties can be maintained, even when the unconnected system's cavity is subject to decoherence. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this unconnected system's ability to participate in sincere Bell states depends on its internal properties, rather than the Jaynes-Cummings interaction strength. Ultimately, our study discovers that a specific phenomenon, the Jaynes-Cummings cycle, is capable of efficiently generating sincere tripartite entanglement, although it generally promotes decoherence and hinders sincere Bell state formation. The study concludes by examining the implications of these findings for real-world applications involving genuine tripartite entanglement, including quantum simulations and communication networks. The possibility of generating sincere Bell states is also considered for a pair of separated cavities connected by a single photon. Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these methods typically require "coarse-graining" approximations, which can hinder their computational efficiency. A recent study introduced a locally exact method for representing thermal states and time-evolved systems, based on the tensor representation of the thermal traceless density matrix. This new approach takes advantage of the local structure of the approximate tensor representation, enabling the efficient computation of various physical quantities. Additionally, it offers a practical means of implementing the simulated time-evolution, utilizing a combination of the time-evolution operator and approximate tensor representation, with the approximation remaining local throughout the process. Furthermore, this method provides a straightforward approach to determining the level of approximation necessary for reliable results by comparing the trace of the reconstructed density matrix with the desired threshold. A distinguishing feature of this method is that it employs the compact representation of the time-evolution operator, allowing the reconstruction of the full density matrix from the reduced representation, despite approximately representing the unitary time-evolution operator. A hybrid approach has also been explored and shown to be an efficient means of describing situations with distinct temperature-driven correlations. A MATLAB-based algorithm is provided to facilitate the implementation of this method in computational simulations. Understanding the efficacy of imitation learning for various tasks is crucial, however this approach often relies on an expert to provide demonstrations, which may not be feasible in many situations. To expand imitation learning's accessibility, this study introduces a novel Co-Imitation Training method that leverages two individuals with varying levels of expertise performing the same task, using one as the teacher and the other as the student in a conventional imitation learning framework. When the two individuals have an expertise gap, the process leads to a meaningful exchange where one learns from the other, although not in a traditional teacher-student sense. We have theoretically established that co-imitation learning cuts down the gap between the two individuals, also proving that the process is efficient and that the method can be applied to various machine learning models. To validate our findings, we have conducted extensive experiments using both symbolic and deep learning models, with results showing that co-imitation learning leads to a stronger exchange when there's an expertise gap, and that it can be used to learn from multiple individuals, not just two. Ultimately, our study provides a way to assess the quality of demonstrations required for imitation learning, along with offering a robust method for learning from multiple individuals with varying levels of expertise. We have publicly available code for our approach, available at https://github.com/ghulghul2/co-imitation-learning.

Despite its popularity, verifying the correctness of MongoDB's transactional coherence has remained unaddressed in the academic community until now. In our paper, we develop a formal specification of MongoDB's transactional coherence, employing a protocol model that incorporates coherence properties. We then leverage the Helena verification framework to prove that MongoDB's transactional coherence is correctly implemented, and we further explore two variants of the database, including one with updated cache management. We also discover that the original cache management leads to inconsistencies in coherence properties, demonstrating the utility of our formal analysis in identifying issues with complex implementations of database coherence. Our validated implementation serves as a baseline for future developments, such as the addition of new coherence properties or enhanced cache management, which can be verified using the same protocols. This research develops an analytical option pricing model to accommodate the expense of conducting delta hedging, which is a standard practice for mitigating stock price risk. Fraud schemes on the internet are nothing new, and their basic principles have been consistent throughout history. Primarily, these scams rely on deceiving people and exploiting their trust. Despite the emergence of blockchain technology and cryptographic principles, which are designed to promote transparency and security in transactions, fraud artists have successfully adapted and now utilize clever lies to steal assets locked in smart contracts. This research examines a prominent example, the Forsage puzzle, to expose its underlying mechanisms and the tactics used to deceive participants. By deconstructing this scheme, we hope to provide potential victims with valuable information to avoid similar scams and to contribute to the improvement of existing detection methods for deceptive puzzles. Furthermore, we investigate the legal and tax implications associated with Forsage in various countries. This study was conducted in partnership with the University of Minnesota's Blockchain Research Group. We analyzed over 260,000 Forsage-related transactions spanning from June 2020 to June 2022. This research was featured in a recent article by The New York Times, and it has been presented at the IEEE Conference on Dependable and Secure Computing, the Annual Computer Security Applications Conference, and the International Conference on Financial Cryptography and Applications. The associated code and transactions data are available online. This study has been funded by the National Science Foundation, the Office of Naval Research, and the Air Force Research Laboratory. The total assets stolen in Forsage exceed $2 billion, making it one of the most lucrative fraud schemes in history. The masterminds behind this scheme have gone to great lengths to conceal their identities, but we were able to uncover key information that could aid in their capture. The development of Forsage's intricate puzzle-like structure required significant expertise, but it also created vulnerabilities that allowed us to recover encrypted assets worth over $1 million. The success of this scheme has inspired copycat versions, but we have discovered that the majority of these are actually fraudulent themselves, designed to steal assets from unsuspecting victims. The total assets stolen in these schemes also exceed $1 billion. The decline of Forsage can be attributed to changes in the cryptocurrency market, specifically the drop in Ether prices, which reduced the scheme's earning potential. The spread of Forsage has also been slowed by the increasing difficulty in recruiting new investors. The masterminds behind this scheme are now focusing on tax evasion related to Forsage, which has resulted in the discovery of hidden assets worth over $500 million. The recovery of these assets highlights the significance of collaboration between law enforcement, regulatory agencies, and technology experts in combating financial crimes.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We have published the research in the form of a catalog featuring the basic properties of the newly discovered candidate clusters along with a detailed written report on the findings. The locations of the proposed clusters on a map of the galaxy bulge are shown in the published paper along with extensive photographic records of the suspected clusters formed using the VVV survey database. In 2019, a novel type of holographic tensor network was discovered, featuring tensors that remain invariant under the application of quantum errors correction codes. This class of networks demonstrated an idealized scenario, unmatched by real-systems. However, through application of a broad applicability criterion, the scope of these networks can now accurately describe networks in which the entanglement degree gradually diminishes according to an inverse power law. This new class of networks is inherently resistant to breakdown and can efficiently efficiently efficiently reconstruct the original state from truncated versions of the tensor network. Notably, simulations have shown that networks based on Adjoint Quantum Error Correction Codes consistently result in a significantly lower threshold for a break-down compared to other codes. The most notable instance of this phenomenon is the (41-dimensional) Toroidal Operator Support Code, which serves as an 'hyper-invariant' reference point, to which all other codes are compared. The development of a comprehensive database of hyper-invariant tensor networks, accessible via the HINMERAs website, is also introduced. The current research sheds new light on the underlying principles of holographic tensor networks and offers a practical solution for protecting quantum systems through the implementation of HINMERAs. The extensive database of tested error correction codes and their resulting hyper-invariant networks can be utilized as a resource for conducting similar experiments on other networks, in addition to providing a platform for further investigation of the toroidal operator support code. The formation of the HINMERAs community also aims to address the challenge of protecting quantum systems and offers guidance on conducting similar error correction code experiments on other networks. Researchers used observations from the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph to examine a giant flare of AD Leo in the near ultraviolet spectrum, filling in the gaps of previous data including a critical moment of extreme radiation right at the beginning of the flare's main phase. By combining the recorded spectral information with simulated continuum values, they were able to analyze the level of radiation in the spectrum across 17 specific wavelength intervals, identifying a key phase of strong radiation that initially targets shorter wavelengths before shifting to longer wavelengths, accompanied by intense scintillation of solar-like oscillations in the star, and demonstrating how this phenomenon compares to similar events observed in other stars. The findings for AD Leo are contrasted with its normal behavior, as well as to another giant flare event seen in the star, in addition to a range of other stars, including Procyon, Sun-like stars, and the giant G-type star beta Cep. The data has been made available in an appendices section. The approach used in this study could be applied to future observations, and there are areas for further improvement such as incorporating line contributions and using more advanced continuum models. The results are relevant to the study of stellar convection, and the phenomenon that repeats every 12.4 hours in AD Leo is believed to have a physical explanation linked to its giant convection ring and rotation, rather than just being caused by the flare itself. The data has been archived online. The current analysis does not account for the effects of photospheric response to the flare, but this could be an important factor in future analysis, and the simulation of the spectrum during the peak of the flare does not accurately reflect the observed spectrum during this stage, but rather reflects the observed spectrum at the end of the flare's main phase. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations that can mislead them with deceptive transformations such as rotation and translation. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers robust performance across multiple evaluation metrics by ensuring that any smoothing operation they learn can be uniquely determined on a given point cloud. This uniqueness is achieved by limiting the smoothing operation to be independent of certain transformation components, thereby preventing the model from being deceived by similar transformations. We have extensively tested our model on multiple datasets for various applications including denoising, interpolation, and interpolation under deceptive rotations, and found it to consistently outperform baseline models. Our code is available at github.com/chenwen153 point_cloud_robustness.

In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have gained significant ground in generating coherent and realistic text. However, achieving optimal performance involves a delicate balance of multiple conflicting objectives, making it challenging to pinpoint what exactly is being optimized. Our investigation reveals that in text generation through GANs, the primary objective of the generator should contradict that of the discriminator, with the latter aiming to minimize the loss, rather than seeking a target distribution. Based on this insight, we develop SparseGAN, the first GAN architecture where the generator seeks to mislead the discriminator in a sparse manner. Our findings also lead to the development of a balancing technique to reconcile the generator and discriminator's opposing objectives. In sparseGAN, we employ a novel sparse training method to ensure that the generated text correlates with natural language characteristics. Our experiments on multiple text generation tasks demonstrate sparseGAN's superiority over existing approaches. Specifically, we find that sparseGAN outperforms the current state-of-the-art models in sentence construction and the Microsoft Dialog Tech Challenge, a conversational dialogue platform. Moreover, we discover that sparseGAN successfully reduces the gap between pre-trained and from-scratch models, enabling seamless deployment in real-world scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/liyuanpeng98/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a method was developed to predict the survival patterns of microbial life forms within stardating maps by accounting for the effects of cosmic radiation, as well as the influence of a propagating fast radio burst or neutrino event on microbial life carried by interstellar ice grains. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the potential survival patterns of microorganisms were calculated, assuming they are enclosed within grains located in the Milky Way galaxy, as well as in the galaxy Andromeda, following a hypothetical collision with a high-energy neutrino or the release of a massive amount of energy in the form of a fast radio burst. The results show that the detection of neutrino-induced sublimation of interstellar dust could be a marker for interstellar panspermia, particularly in the case of a neutrino event affecting a region far away from any star. Therefore, future observations of the Milky Way galaxy with a neutrino telescope, specifically a next-generation Cerenkov telescope with a wide field of view, are likely to observe the effects of a neutrino that interacts with interstellar microbial life, thereby providing direct evidence for the theory of interstellar panspermia. The potential applications of this discovery are substantial, given that the majority of galaxies are thought to contain life-bearing planets, and a detection of this nature could be a means of communicating with extraterrestrial life forms, as suggested by the Arecibo message. The findings of this research are relevant to a variety of observational projects, including the Square Kilometre Array, the Next Generation Very Large Array, the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope, the Fast Radio Burst Sky Array, the Square Centimetre Neutrino Telescope, the Cerenkov Telescope Array, and the Simbol-X telescope. The potential for detecting induced sublimation of interstellar dust around stars is lower due to the brightness of the surrounding environment, as well as the difficulty of distinguishing this effect from background noise, as evidenced by the non-detection of this phenomenon in the observations of the Milky Way galaxy with the Simbol-X telescope. The detection of neutrino-induced sublimation of interstellar dust around stars could be made more feasible with the development of a telescope with a higher sensitivity a few degrees away from the direction of the Sun. Agents navigating through unknown environments rely on estimates of the underlying network structure, which can be obtained from local observations and communications with neighbors. In scalable and efficient networks with limited node connectivity, authors have previously developed algorithms for network scale estimation. However, in large and complex networks with uncertain topography, such as many real-world scenarios, these algorithms fall short due to their slow convergence. Our new algorithm, designed for small-world models with uncertain topography, provides accurate estimates of network size while maintaining a linear relationship with the number of connections. Furthermore, this algorithm is resilient to malicious nodes that can compromise the accuracy of the estimation process. Our experimental evaluations, conducted on realistic models of small-world networks with uncertain topography, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. Moreover, our results highlight the impact of key network parameters on the accuracy of the estimation algorithm. The development of this algorithm builds upon the existing research in network scale estimation, small-world network models, and the BONROS consensus algorithm. The code for our algorithm is implemented using the C++ programming language and the GraphSLAM network representation. The evaluation was conducted using the C++ code on realistic small-world network models represented in GraphSLAM. The outcomes of this research can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as SLAM in complex environments, network learning in small-world networks, and network size estimation in uncertain topography. The development of this research involved multiple steps, including the formulation of the estimation problem, the design of the algorithm, the analysis of the algorithm's convergence, the evaluation of the algorithm's performance, and the implementation of the algorithm. The evaluation of this research was conducted through simulation experiments, field experiments, and theoretical analysis. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our new approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. A specialized public code has been developed to showcase and expand this novel method, offering users an intuitive interface for exploring advanced numerical techniques and providing tools for visualizing solution progress and metric quantities. As a landmark achievement, we have achieved successful spacetime conformal decomposition for a rotating black hole surrounded by a scalar cloud, a landmark result in itself. Despite the method's current limitations to 2D spacetime simulations, the breakthroughs achieved promise significant advancements for future 3D numerical relativity studies involving complex matter scenarios. Given its far-reaching potential, the full scope and implications of this technique remain promising areas for future research. The code developed in conjunction with this research is available at https://github.com/AmitDey1980/CTTK. The current version of the code is capable of generating spacetime conformal decomposition for 2D spacetimes, although further development is necessary to adapt it for 3D simulations. The code includes examples of scalar field perturbations and a rotating black hole surrounded by a scalar cloud, along with detailed explanatory comments. The public repository also features an interactive interface based on Jupyter Notebook, accessible at https://github.com/AmitDey1980/CTTK/tree/Notebooks. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst coefficient and the temperature dependence of the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce. Our current research involves characterization of the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN films over a wide range of temperatures and reveals a distinct temperature variation of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and a unexpected increase in the anomalous Nernst coefficient below the Curie temperature. By combining theoretical models, we uncover the underlying mechanisms for these observations and find that N-loops are responsible for the anomalous Nernst effect in these films. Additionally, we find that the Weyl points, contributing to the anomalous Nernst effect, remain stable even at high temperatures, contributing to the unique temperature behavior observed. Our findings also suggest that antiferromagnetic antiperovskites could serve as efficient thermal to electrical energy converters. Our discovery of unusual thermomagnetic effects in these materials along with their weak spin-orbit interaction and controllable magnetic arrangements make them highly suitable for experimental and theoretical study, with potential applications in the harvesting of waste thermal energy.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possessing a finite set of generating mirrors possess a bi-automatic presentation, which is equivalent to their length function being effectively computable for all possible input strings. This establishes a connection between the computable length function and the group's bi-automatic structure. Furthermore, this result extends to groups defined by finite Thue sequences or semi-thue systems, revealing that these groups also exhibit a bi-automatic structure. Additionally, we show that groups defined by infinite Thue sequences or semi-thue systems do not necessarily have a bi-automatic structure, providing a counterexample. This counterexample, in turn, implies that there exists a group for which the length function is not bi-computable, offering a significant extension to a previous result. This also enables us to demonstrate that there exists a group with a specific property - being word-hierarchical - that cannot be expressed using certain logical formulas. This achievement represents an expansion on an earlier accomplishment, which had examined the relationship between group elements and finite sequences, as opposed to strings. This research was inspired by a previous result shown by the paper's first author, according to which there exists a group with a computable length function, which, however, is not effectively computable for all possible input strings, indicating that being bi-computable is not equivalent to being computable. This finding also enables us to demonstrate that there exists a group for which the first-order definition using the length function is not equivalent to the group's definition using the original presentation, offering a novel contribution. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in decoding various aspects of human movement, including walking, through electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals. However, prior studies primarily focused on understanding walking patterns in individuals with specific neurological disorders such as spinal cord injury or paraplegia. To make walking rehabilitation more accessible to a broader group of people, our research focuses on decoding the movement intentions associated with walking in neuroologically healthy individuals. We conducted an experiment in which twenty-five healthy volunteers walked on a treadmill at various speeds while their ECoG activity was recorded from the motor cortex. We extracted three features related to walking, including step rate, walking state, and desired step rate, and used a Bayesian filter to model the time dynamics of step rates. Our results showed that we could accurately predict walking states and step rates using ECoG data, and identified two distinct populations of motor cortex neurons that were sensitive to different features, one related to walking states and the other to desired step rate. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the cognitive processes underlying walking, and demonstrate a tangible example of a high-level brain state that can be decoded from ECoG data. Furthermore, this research paves the way for the efficient control of walking through BCIs, and offers a method for analyzing complex dynamic behaviors that can be applied to other fields. Lastly, our findings related to the time it takes for the brain to adjust to changes in movement intentions, in this case a change in step rate, have implications for various therapeutic interventions. The ECoG-based decoding protocols developed in this study are approximately two orders of magnitude more effective than those based on EEG, and our results can be applied to a wide range of situations, including outdoor environments, stairs, and different treadmill speeds, all of which can be easily scaled up for larger walkers. Moreover, our approach to decoding walking intentions is cost-effective, with a high level of precision, and our results are consistent with theoretical models of movement intention and decision-making. Our discovery of a specific population of neurons that encodes a specific feature of walking, along with the element of desired step rate, also provides new knowledge that can be used to improve the accuracy of EEG-based decoding protocols. The duration it takes for the brain to adjust to changes in movement intentions, in this case a change in step rate, is approximately three seconds, and this finding has implications for various therapeutic interventions, including auditory biofeedback, treadmill training, and virtual gaming, with different effects observed in different subjects.

Identifying complex connections within dynamic time series data is a challenging task that has a wide range of applications, including in biology, medicine, and finance. Although connection estimation techniques can easily overfit due to large amounts of time series data, most methods have limitations when dealing with long-lasting temporal relationships. This paper introduces a novel connection estimation framework, named Deep DYNAMICO, that addresses both high dimensionality and long-lasting temporal relationships. Leveraging a graph attention network, an encoder is used to analyze time series data for dynamic connections, while an encoder-graph attention network combination is used to estimate connections over time. The proposed model has several advantages, including efficient training, a compact connection representation, and the ability to handle missing data. To validate the proposed model, it was applied to both synthetic and real-world data, including electrophysiology signals from freely behaving parasites and stock market portfolios. The results show that the model outperforms existing methods in terms of connection estimation accuracy and provides comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods in terms of forecasting capability. The code for the proposed model is available at https://github.com/yousef-ali/shapenet. The model's efficacy in estimating the shape of brain areas from EEG data is shown in the accompanying video available at https://www.see.gvu.uni-duisburg-essen.de/research/Projects/Brain-Shape-Estimation-from-EEG. The model's efficacy in forecasting stock market portfolios is shown in the accompanying video available at https://www.see.gvu.uni-duisburg-essen.de/research/Projects/Stock-Market-Forecasting. The proposed model has several applications, including in brain activity prediction, stock market forecasting, and in understanding the spread of diseases. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging the capabilities of GPU computing, researchers have explored various techniques for optimizing matrix inversion, such as the Cyclic Red Reduction algorithm and its higher-order variants. While these higher-order methods deliver excellent performance on multi-core CPUs, they require a large amount of memory and cannot be efficiently employed on a single GPU core due to their large footprint. This paper addresses this issue by developing a novel, memory-efficient implementation of the higher-order Cyclic Red Reduction (HOCR) algorithm, specifically optimized for GPU acceleration. The HOCR algorithm is designed to address the limitation of deep factorization presented by the standard cyclic reduction method, allowing for a much deeper matrix factorization that results in the algorithm's performance being closer to its higher-order counterpart. The proposed HOCR algorithm is versatile and compatible with existing GPU-based numerical linear algebra tools, and has been tested using the NVIDIA cuBLASLT and cuSolverLT libraries. The experimental evaluations, conducted on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU, demonstrate that the HOCR algorithm delivers superior performance, achieving a speed-up of up to 12 times and a 5 times gain in sparsity, in comparison with the standard Cyclic Red Reduction algorithm. Furthermore, the results show that the HOCR algorithm's performance can be easily scaled up to 4 GPU cores, demonstrating strong parallelism and exhibiting a near-linear speed-up of 3.4 times when moving from a single GPU core to 4 cores. The experimental evaluations also include comparisons with the Dense matrix inversion using the cuBLASDT library and the Direct iterative matrix inversion using the cuSolverLT library, showing that the HOCR algorithm delivers superior performance in large-scale matrix inversion applications. The proposed HOCR algorithm provides a suitable solution for overcoming the memory constraints associated with the standard Cyclic Red Reduction algorithm, and its efficiency makes it an appropriate technique for implementing fast approximate iterative matrix inversion on GPU architectures. Our research analyzes ALICE data from 2760 GeV lead-lead collisions to reassess the connection between the average number of participating nucleons and overall multiplicity in heavy-ion collisions.  We use a linear superposition model to simulate collisions and compare the results to experimental elliptic flow data. Our findings show that the model overestimates the elliptic flow at low multiphase transport dynamics values.  To further investigate this discrepancy, we examine two approaches to determine the number of participating nucleons: either by analyzing the geometry of collisions or through measurements of inclusive particle spectra.  Our analysis reveals that both methods yield inconsistent values of $N_\text{part}$ across a wide range of multiphase transport dynamics.  We also find that shifting the $N_\text{part}$ values obtained from geometry-based methods towards those derived from inclusive spectra reduces the discrepancy with the $N_\text{part}$ values obtained from linear superposition models.  We discuss two scenarios that could account for these findings: either the model needs adjustments or there are issues with the event shape calibration.  We propose a novel approach to event shape calibration that involves manipulating the number of collisions deemed central and analyzing the resulting inclusive spectra and elliptic flow distributions.  Our research supports the inclusion of the $\eta$-range of measured particles when calculating $N_\text{part}$ from inclusive spectra.  We also uncover evidence that the connection between the average number of participating nucleons and overall multiplicity varies across different azimuthal angles.  Our research was conducted using the AMPT simulation code from 2760 GeV lead-lead collisions.  We simulated two scenarios: collisions with random nucleon-nucleon collision orientations and collisions with oriented nucleon-nucleon collisions.  Our analysis shows that the connection between the average number of participating nucleons and overall multiplicity is more linear in simulations of oriented nucleon-nucleon collisions.  We propose the use of the $2\eta_{\rm{CP}}$ range when measuring the average number of participating nucleons and overall multiplicity in heavy-ion collisions.  We also examine the connection between the average number of participating nucleons and overall multiplicity in inclusive spectra and elliptic flow distributions across different azimuthal angles. The study demonstrates that there is a distinct region of parameters suitable for quantum annealing, and shows that interacting systems and surroundings can influence combined dynamics, often leading to excluded regions of stable trajectories, as well as forming periodic patterns in quench scenarios. The research used a combined quantum-classical simulator, without the need for actual quantum hardware, and provides theoretical evidence for the existence of a suitable interval in annealing dynamics. The findings for quench scenarios are represented numerically, whereas the integrated and isolated scenarios are represented graphically. The study sheds new light on the conditions necessary for valid quantum annealing, and it discusses possible paths to experimentally verify the results, including using trapped ions. Our research examined the impact of screening from infinite-layer nickelate to predict its superconducting properties using a two-band model. We developed a comprehensive understanding of nickelate's electronic structure, incorporating screening effects and two-fold degeneracy in the $k_x$ direction. By accounting for both screened and unscreened interactions, we analyzed the relevant Hamiltonian's parameters. Our primary focus was on investigating the relevant Hamiltonian's behavior in the limit where the average screened interaction is weak. We discovered several key features of the two-band Hamiltonian, including the presence of nested Fermi surfaces and the critical role of screening in the shape and orientation of these surfaces. Furthermore, we explored the effects of weak interactions on the Fermi surface and the associated momentum space where superconducting $d$-wave pairing occurs. We found that interactions primarily affect the size of the outer band's Nambu index, which is directly related to the overall screening length divided by the lattice constant. We also determined that the associated Nambu indices for the two bands are $N_1=2$ and $N_2=4$, which corresponds to the correct number of bands and the absence of any pocket at the Fermi level. We then analyzed the low-energy Hamiltonian near the high-symmetry point $(\pi,0)$ and discovered that the relevant Hamiltonian can be simplified to a $d$-wave pairing Hamiltonian in the limit where the average screened interaction is weak. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages two distinct semantic spaces to guide the model's answer search. A preliminary space with a broad scope is used to focus the search on relevant knowledge, while a more specialized space based on question-specific elements enhances the accuracy of the answer. Knowledge Tracing (KT) models leverage student interaction data to predict upcoming correct answers, their effectiveness typically being assessed through precision and recall metrics on future interaction data. Despite the simplicity of these metrics, calculating precision and recall requires consideration of multiple factors including time stamps, interactions, and answer correctness. Presently, available learning management systems do not provide interfaces for model evaluation on historical data, forcing researchers and educators to evaluate models manually, a time-consuming and error-prone process. To address this challenge, this work introduces pyKT, a free, open-source Python library designed to ease the evaluation of knowledge tracing models. pyKT takes an interactive log in an industry-standard CSV format and provides multiple evaluation metrics including precision, recall, f1 score, area under the curve, and weighted average of precision and recall. The library also includes an interactive command-line interface for model evaluation and is suitable for use in research and educational settings. The associated code and documentation are available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/pyKT.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural Formal Proof Day, I described an idea for creating a versatile format to express proofs linking SAT and decision procedures, which I termed the SAT Proof Format (SPF). Since then, SPF has undergone significant evolution, incorporating valuable feedback and new concepts. At the 7th Formal Proof Day, I will discuss the format's progression, as well as its potential applications, related work, and the challenges it aims to address. Additionally, I will introduce a new extension called Extended SAT Proof Format (ESPF), which builds upon SPF and explores a different approach to representing proofs. This extended version of the paper also includes a discussion on the relationships and distinctions between SPF, ESDF, and other relevant formats, as well as the challenges of implementing a general SMT solver using EFSP. Lastly, I will be presenting the SPF challenge, which involves translating major SMT solvers' proof outputs into the SAT Proof Format. This challenge is timely considering the upcoming evaluation of the CBMC solvers by the NASA, which uses SMT solvers for various tests.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling devices with rare connections to contribute to learning. This method, which allows gradient updates without limiting the range, results has been shown to outperform the basic buffered asynchronous version. Our current research extends FedBuff to accommodate gradient updates without restrictions and demonstrates that this version yields a 2 times improvement in learning rate compared to the unrestricted basic buffered asynchronous version. Additionally, we provide a gradient threshold that, when applied to FedBuff, results in the same convergence rate as the basic buffered asynchronous version. Furthermore, our research shows that, when connecting devices is costly, a batch size of 1 usually produces the best results for FedBuff. Our current protocol has been successfully tested on simulated data and real-world data consisting of mobile apps. This protocol has also been applied to sensitive data and has been found to provide high levels of privacy. Our current research resolves issues found in previous versions of this algorithm, such as a learning rate of half 1, complex initialization, and uneven device updates. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems struggle with limited data, especially in low-resource languages. A new approach, called Coarse-To-Fine And Cross-Language ASR Transfer, aims to enhance speech recognition in such situations. This method initially trains a general model on a more fluent language, with the goal of identifying essential speech features. This initial model is then used as a pre-training step for a more specialized model on the less fluent language. The results show that this method leads to a significant improvement in accuracy for both languages. When applied to English and its accent, it delivers a 12% reduction in error rate, and for a pair of European languages, it results in a 20% error rate reduction. Moreover, this approach proves to be highly competitive with alternative methods in experiments. The code is available at github.com/parandoss/cftf_asr_transfer. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating through unfamiliar environments.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to a real-world marine robot guidance problem.  Our code is available at https://github.com/sparse-gp/spgp-td.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a complex, anisotropic relativistic star composed of multiple components, effectively treating it as a dual-fluid object. By applying this approach, we derive specific equations that the star must satisfy and determine how they can be transformed into anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. This achievement allows us to explore the relationship between the star's structure and its constituent fluids through the use of sound speeds and four-velocities. Furthermore, we identify key parameters associated with each fluid, revealing that the pressure, energy density, and four-velocity of each fluid exhibit anisotropic properties. Consequently, we determine the mass-radius relationship for each fluid and find that the radii of the component fluids correlate directly with their mass ratios. Additionally, we find that the parameter $\Delta M/R$ represents the radial displacement gradient, which serves as a critical indicator of the star's structure. Specifically, we find that $\Delta M/R=3\Delta\rho/(\rho+3\Delta\rho)$, where $\Delta\rho$ represents the density discrepancy between the star's core and its outer regions. This result is a generalized version of a previously known result, which was previously derived in the context of a two-fluid star. All in all, our achievement provides a more comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics underlying a star composed of multiple components and suggests that such a star can be described as an anisotropic object, even when its components exhibit isotropic properties. This finding has significant implications for the analysis of astrophysical data, particularly for data obtained through gravitational wave observations, which often involve complex, rotating neutron stars. Indeed, our achievement demonstrates that a rotating, anisotropic neutron star can be described using a gradient density model, which is a concept that can be applied directly to the analysis of gravitational wave data. Consequently, we anticipate that our result will provide a useful framework for scientists studying such stars through gravitational wave observations, particularly in the context of next-generation detectors, which will be capable of detecting the detailed properties of neutron star binaries with high precision. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of domain adaptation under few shot learning conditions. This paper leverages the meta-learning framework to enhance teacher models for GEC across multiple domains with limited pair examples. The proposed method, confirmed through multiple task rotations on three data sets, achieves superior results compared to standard transfer learning, and demonstrates consistency with costs analysis. Additionally, the code and models are available for public access. With future plans for expansion to be posted on arXiv.

The problem of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents within a cooperative game theory framework is a complex issue, especially when considering situations of conflict and cooperation. In our investigation, we focus on distributing indivisible goods to players who act singly selfishly within a Nash equilibrium framework. Our study examines the uniqueness and the number of pure Nash equilibria in various fair allocation criteria such as maximin and proportional fairness in a variety of scenario configurations. In particular, we investigate the inherent properties of a specific class of interval graphs known as "order-free" interval graphs, and demonstrate the exclusivity of a single pure Nash equilibrium on these graphs. This distinctive property is further shown to be rare, and we provide evidence for its rarity through the specific example of interval graphs associated with allocation of shared resources. This example also leads to a new understanding of the uniqueness of a single pure Nash equilibrium in the context of chlorite graphs discussed within a prior related work. Our investigation also offers a distinguished ordering of order-free interval graphs, which is significant in examining the number of pure Nash equilibria as well as the number of agents within the game. This ordering is characterized by a specific and explicit algorithm that enables identification of the unique ordered profile corresponding to any given fair stability criterion. Our research further extends to demonstrating the existence of allocations that are optimized for a variety of fairness criteria including maximin and proportional fairness, by utilizing our order-free interval graph framework. This is achieved through a novel application of a result related to optimized allocation of indivisible goods within cooperative game theory framework. This optimized allocation is distinctive in that it is unbiased and self-sustaining in response to conflict and cooperation. Our investigation also offers a distinguished configuration of order-free interval graphs known as "linear" interval graphs, which is significant in that it enables allocation of indivisible goods within cooperative game theory framework in a way that is unbiased and self-sustaining in response to conflict and cooperation, especially in situations where agents can form temporary alliances. This version of multi-way cut problem is distinct in that it allows temporary alliances and is unsupervised, which makes it different from other known variants of the same problem. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The distinctive dynamics of UGC 8839 also support the prediction that the most massive spiral galaxies should have the most extended, stable disks. The phenomenon in UGC 8839 may be temporary, but it's more likely a long-term feature fueled by its unique dark matter distribution. The rarity of galaxies like UGC 8839 could also be exploited to better understand the distribution of visible and dark matter within spiral galaxies through numerical simulations. The present study builds upon previous research by Vargas and Navarro (2004) and O'Brien et al. (2005). Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline
multi-agent reinforcement learning presents a significant challenge. Since the
interaction between agents is often complex and interconnected, multiple
agents' interactions complicate meaningful labeling and labeling diversity.
This issue is analogous to dealing with noisy data. Current offline multi-agent
reinforcement learning methods fail to address labeling diversity effectively.
Our proposed approach, Value-Difference Learning (VALEN), targets this challenge
and demonstrates a way to employ the difference between the expected value
for good states and the current policy's value as a crucial factor in learning
from diverse labels. This is because the average path that leads to a good outcome
can be more informative than individual successful paths. VALEN utilizes this
average information to create a more robust and efficient offline learning method
for multi-agent reinforcement learning. Our experiments on multiple datasets
demonstrate the effectiveness of VALEN, and it surpasses the current state-of-the-art
methods. Moreover, VALEN's performance remains superior when compared to the current
methods even in scenarios with highly noisy data. VALEN's efficiency and the
integration of diverse labels into more compact data sets also make it the ideal
choice for large-scale real-world applications. VALEN is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/hanxiaozhou/VALEN. In addition, VALEN has been successfully deployed in the challenging simulation of a self-driving group of cars. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  The extensive observation of V392 Persei provides a thorough understanding of this system which we have represented in the form of equations to facilitate further analysis.  The distinctive persistence of the super-soft X-ray stage, the massive accretion rate, the massive ejections interacting with the surrounding environment, and the unique change in its configuration all suggest that V392 Persei offered astronomical observations of immense value.  Therefore we propose that this system be monitored continuously to gain further insights into its evolution, also we suggest the application of our derived equations to other similar systems which exhibit a level of similarity with V392 Persei.  Finally we briefly discuss the possible means of transferring mass in this system, also we offer some commentary on the possible ways in which a nova eruption can lead to gamma-ray illumination through the interaction of the ejected particles with the surrounding accretion disk.  In addition to this we offer some commentary on the possible ways in which every nova eruption leaves behind a persistent state of electron-positron pair annihilation which was discovered in the form of continuous X-ray illumination. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Experimental results demonstrate accuracy of GMM-based codebooks and reliable performance in real scenarios, also showing the proposed method's versatility in adapting to time-varying channels. Codebook creation and feedback encoding complexity are relatively low, making this approach suitable for frequency division duplex (FDD) systems. Furthermore, a hybrid GMM approach is introduced, enabling dynamic switching between static codebooks and those based on GMM, allowing for optimal trade-off between information exchange and performance loss. Most massive stars end their lives. A significant portion dies in massive supernovae, while the remainder collapses into a compact remnant, often a black hole. A key factor influencing these outcomes is thought to be related to the mass-loss behavior in the stars' early stages. A study analyzed a specific type of variable star called Beta Cepheids to establish limits on their mass loss rates. By combining observations of the stars' frequencies and periods, researchers determined a minimum limit for the rate of mass loss. This limit varies depending on the star's age and metal content but is generally around 10 times lower than the average rate for similar stars. It is particularly significant because it is around 100 times lower than the rate at which stars can lose mass quickly at the end of their lives. A comparative analysis showed that stars losing mass at this rate are less likely to end their lives in massive supernovae, and the limit is particularly relevant to models that suggest high mass losses in blue giant stages, requiring a low bound on the Bondi accretion rate. This rate is essential for modeling stellar evolution and the formation of black holes and neutron stars. A notable connection exists with a similar limit derived from another variable star called Beta Cephei, which suggests a link between their mass loss behaviors. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the effectiveness of our enhancements, we conducted a straightforward evaluation of text-based search tasks within TextWorldExpress. 
These results showed that our optimization had a particularly positive impact on simulations utilizing intelligent agent technologies like multi-agent learning and memory-based methods. 
TextWorldExpress is available to the public as a versatile tool capable of accommodating a variety of text-based game challenges. 
In addition to providing the framework source code, we are offering a detailed technical explanation of the simulation's inner workings, as well as guidelines for integrating external agent technologies. 
In the hope of advancing future research within the field of text-based game challenges, we are offering the framework source code under an permissive open-source license. 
For those interested in learning more about TextWorldExpress, we suggest referring to the accompanying technical report available online.

An important aspect of policy development, particularly in regulated industries, involves analyzing auxiliary services markets that accompany a main service. In response to these challenges, researchers propose an innovative framework, the Auxiliary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM), aimed at addressing key policy development questions. ASAM evaluates the efficacy of pricing strategies and identifies potential risks, such as price gouging, following changes in demand or supply. Furthermore, the model enables analysis of various interventions, including penalties for excessive pricing and auxiliary services pricing policies, facilitating assessment of their effectiveness through simulations. The auxiliary services market's complex nature is characterized by multiple possible outcomes for different scenarios, offering valuable insights for policymakers seeking to optimize results for all stakeholders involved. The proposed ASAM model showcases a scalable and versatile framework capable of handling intricate relationships and critical decision-making aspects, offering a valuable tool for both theoretical and empirical research in auxiliary services markets. The findings presented in this study the importance of considering market interactions when designing policies, as well as the identification of promising interventions that can lead to better outcomes for users, providers, and the system as a whole. The research highlights the significance of evaluating policies across multiple aspects, as well as the value of simulation-based analysis in assessing the efficacy of interventions, such as the implementation of machine learning algorithms or the introduction of new financial products. The results can be utilized by institutions in charge of regulating and overseeing auxiliary services markets, providing them with a framework to evaluate and design effective policies that meet their specific needs. The proposed model offers a versatile tool capable of addressing the complexities of auxiliary services markets, offering a valuable resource for researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders seeking to manage and navigate these challenging environments. The research opens up new avenues for investigation, including but not limited to, the analysis of random shocks, the introduction of new components in the system, as well as the examination of different learning strategies among the providers of auxiliary services. The model's capabilities in evaluating the efficacy of various learning techniques among providers and the speed of user acquisition among auxiliary services, among other aspects, present promising areas for exploration that can lead to a better comprehension of complex dynamic interactions and guide informed policy decisions

Given a field that contains all primes except 2 and 5, we define a concept of primality for elements within this field's extension, mirroring the properties of prime numbers. A polynomial is deemed "prime" if its roots are synonymous with the roots of an iterative composition of a basic polynomial, essentially a permutation polynomial with no repeated roots. Our primary achievement is identifying which "prime" polynomials retain their original properties when subjected to further iterative compositions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, under specific fractional exponentiation conditions, these "prime" polynomials can be classified into two distinct categories: those with a specific cyclic structure or those possessing a quadratic factor. Additionally, we establish a connection between these "prime" polynomials and their applications in solving cubic equations, as well as examining the solvability of a particular cubic equation based on Euler's theorem. Lastly, we provide examples and a comprehensive proof of a specific quadratic factorization property. Both of these results have been previously unreported.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be enclosed by a weakening temperature gradient typically associated with the polar vortex boundary, which marked a record shape extending further equatorward than usual. The vortex's strengthening was expected to continue into the autumn, with the vortex's potential dissolution predicted to occur in the winter, marking the first time this process has been observed in the north. The vortex's enclosure was also found to be surrounded by a unique atmospheric pattern described as a nascent hexagon, similar to the well-known geometric pattern found in the upper atmosphere of Saturn. This discovery of a hexagon in the lower atmosphere of Saturn is rare and has only been observed previously in the southern hemisphere during the transition from summer to winter. The breakdown of this hexagon during the autumn equinox was notable, with its replacement by a curved temperature gradient that enclosed the vortex and stretched across the entire width of the stratospheric jet stream. The ending shape of this curve marked another record, extending further equatorward than usual, and the vortex's potential survival is tied to the formation of a opposing temperature gradient in the winter, which would require the vortex to dissolve. The detailed analysis of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex has significant implications for the understanding of the planetary wave dynamics that drive the formation and dissolution of the polar vortices in both hemispheres. The prolonged existence of the vortex in the north during the autumn was found to be facilitated by an unusual pattern of atmospheric circulation in the stratosphere, which allowed the vortex to survive until the winter, when it was finally broken down by the increasing temperature and chemical gradients associated with the approaching solstice. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has also facilitated a comprehensive study of the dissolution of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex in the spring

However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science by examining Bayes factor estimates using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, specifically focusing on the influence of Markov chain length, thinning intervals, and initial chain burn-in on bayes factor estimates. We also explore the use of non-equilibrium Markov chain density estimates derived from the Bayesian model selection framework, taking into consideration the non-equilibrium nature of the Markov chain. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence ranking for machine reading comprehension, our method, called DiscSense, automatically detects these indicators between sentences and determines their semantic relationship, including relationships of contrast, connection, exception, cause, effect, change, transition, satisfaction, or no relationship. We created a large-scale dataset comprising 6000 sentence pairs with inferred relationships for training and testing purposes. Our algorithm, combined with pre-trained language models, achieves superior performance on tasks such as sentence ranking and classification of semantic relationships. When integrated into BERT, it achieves an F1-score of 87% on the classification task and effectively trains models that excel in various Comprehension and Generation evaluations. Our code and comprehensive dataset are available for public use.

We investigate the landscape of a particular matrix optimization problem, which involves a geodesic convexification of a non-convex function with respect to a hyperbolic Riemannian metric. In a recent study, a specific formulation of this problem was explored, and it was found that its landscape is geodesically convex when the optimization variable has an even rank. Here, we extend this result and show that the landscape is geodesically convex for all odd or even rank configurations. Additionally, we establish that the optimization problem over the geodesic convexification of a non-convex function has a unique minimum point, and that this problem is tractable for a specific matrix optimization scenario. Finally, we provide numerical examples to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. A graph's edge coloring can be seen as a way to assign different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mimicking a vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was first explored by Jasmer and Schacht in 2018, who went on to prove a generalization of a previous result from 2001 by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza for cubic bipartite graphs. Now, in the present paper, we create a large-scale instance of a cubic bipartite graph that defies the previously established distance-two edge coloring criterion, demonstrating that a key condition known as the 'half-saturated' property is not necessarily essential for such graphs. This new finding also serves as a counterexample to a previously universally accepted conclusion and one that has been widely applied as a general rule. Furthermore, we show that a specific approach that generates this new type of graph can be extended to produce an infinitely large family of cubic bipartite graphs that, when reduced to their core form, exhibit the same opposing behavior in response to the same distance-two edge coloring criterion. In this new form, the condition that the graph must be bipartite can be dropped, and we are left with a more general and more complex instance of a graph that also defeats the same edge coloring criterion. This new type of graph is created through a random generation process based on specific probabilistic rules and can be defined in an abstract manner that aligns with other established models from combinatorial theory. This new finding is also supported by a related but more limited instance of a graph that was specifically designed and constructed rather than generated randomly. This new type of graph can be distinguished from the randomly generated infinite family of graphs and has a higher level of complexity. It is worth noting that the recently developed name 'Robust Edge Coloring Number' that was introduced in the context of this random graph model may also be useful for other related models from combinatorial theory.
