Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN implementations. The range control method can be efficiently applied to various CNN deployments, especially those utilizing limited memory. The code for our prototype is available at: https://github.com/SiliconPilot/ActivationRangeSupervision.git. The underlying binary floating point system used in this work is the PULP ISS, a binary floating point processor issued under the Berkeley Software Distribution license. The code for the vehicle dataset is issued under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license. This formula enables us to generate a series of twisted Poincaré algebra variants. We have specifically calculated a number of one-parameter collections of Jordanian twists constructed from the Poincaré algebra basis elements. By utilizing these generated twists, we have developed the associated star product coefficients. Furthermore, we have investigated the limit behavior of these one-parameter collections as they approach specific values, including exponential, hyperbolic, and logarithmic limits. We have also examined the relationship between these twists and the classical Poisson bracket structure. We propose a novel method for creating a unified multi-lingual embedding in a shared semantic space. Our approach uses a cluster-consistent word embedding to incorporate multiple perspectives of similar words across different languages, ensuring that equivalent words maintain the same relative positions in comparison to other words. We employ a mixture of translation methods and multi-lingual embeddings to map words to the shared space, while also utilizing clustering information to guide the embedding process. As a result, our method effectively handles homograph issues that traditional multi-lingual embedding approaches struggle with. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by implementing a range of tasks that leverage multi-lingual clustering, including semantic classification, cross-lingual classification, and multi-lingual document clustering. Our proposed approach achieves superior performance in all cases, surpassing current multi-lingual embedding methods and alternative cluster-based models. We also analyze different components of our method to determine their individual contributions, and discuss potential applications in areas like cross-lingual sentiment analysis and multi- lingual topic modeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/ClusterConsistent.

Our study provides calculations of pion, kaon, proton, and phi-meson production rates in gold-nucleus collisions at a collision energy of 5.44 TeV, using a parton model that takes into account effects of parton shadowing. Specifically, we examine the fabrication rates of these mesons and baryons through collisions, and demonstrate how parton shadowing influences the calculation results. Furthermore, the model enables comparison of fabrication rates in proton-proton collisions, enabling the determination of collision systems in which these particles were fabricated via collisions, rather than being produced directly. This is particularly relevant for exotic collisions such as xenon-xeon collisions at the same energy of 5.44 TeV. This approach allows for identification of the dominant processes by which these particles were fabricated, as well as the contribution of initial state collisions, and is consistent with experimental data obtained during the LHC Run 1. This model predicts the following production ratios in xenon-xeon collisions at 5.44 TeV: total phi-meson production (per nucleon) of 2.58, total kaon production (per nucleon) of 5.73, and total proton production (per nucleon) of 3.73, given parton shadowing values of 0.624 for gluons, 0.378 for valence quarks, and 0.45 for sea quarks. This study also examines the fabrication rates of these mesons and baryons in gold-nucleus collisions at the same energy of 5.44 TeV, finding that the majority of produced pions, kaons, and phi-mesons were fabricated via collisions, as opposed to being produced directly, with production ratios per nucleon of 4.37, 2.03, and 1.03 respectively. Our study introduces new types of regular expression constraints involving the operators '[<]', '[>]', and 'within' in the context of strings and lists. We demonstrate the applicability of these constraints to specific problems, including verifying data formats and validating text patterns. Our decision-making algorithm for solving these constraints leverages a symbolic approach and utilizes a dedicated, extended regular expression library. We evaluate and test our method using a subset of regular expression constraints from the RE2 library, a widely used standard for testing regular expression implementations. Our results show that our method outperforms the approach based on regular expression compilation and execution, mentioned in the related work, and that it effectively handles complex list constraints. Our research also explores various list constraint relaxation scenarios and applies them to validate certain patterns of regular expressions. Our evaluation indicates that these constraints can be solved efficiently, with a notable decrease in size when compared to their string-based counterparts. Our method, available under the Apache License, is suited for general use as a building block for larger applications, and we provide a simple list constraint relaxation implementation as a separate entity. Inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide accurate and real-time orientation and position information, but their state starts unknown and drifts over time. To address these challenges, we investigate deep learning models for visual-inertial localization, specifically using IMUs and a single camera, and propose the EMA-VIO framework with external memory attention. This model initially estimates the initial state and time-varying bias in the inertial measurements, and then uses an external memory to capture the dynamics of the inertial measurements over time. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, yet certain materials exhibit non-linear quantum behavior driven by rotation symmetry, outpacing their linear counterparts. We develop a framework to recognize and characterize non-linear Weyl semimetals in three-dimensional space, identifying a novel category - we call them "square-root" higher-order Weyl materials, whose topological attributes are defined by cubic terms instead of the standard Lorentz-like tensor architecture. A direct comparison with their linear counterparts reveals unique non-linear topological properties, specifically a non-linear equivalent of the Fermi arc, describable by a vector that hinges on the momentum space and exhibits a "Fermi pocket" behavior. Our theoretical findings are further linked to actual materials, specifically a class of transition metal dichalcogenides, where we anticipate the non-linear Weyl behavior in close proximity to an atomic lattice distortion, proposing that layered 2D materials with an atomic lattice distortion along the c-direction may serve as square-root higher-order Weyl materials. Our proposed framework is applied to actual materials, namely Ta$_{1-x}$Nb$_x$Te3, which displays a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal phase along the x-axis within a relatively narrow range. Our calculations predict that this material exhibits a relatively vast area of square-root higher-order Weyl behavior in the Brillouin zone, specifically along the M-K-M' trajectory in the reciprocal space, whichcorresponds to multiple non-linear Fermi arc trajectories, offering an actionable framework for experimental verification. Our findings also suggest that the square-root higher-order Weyl behavior can be influenced by applying an electric field or strain to Ta1-xNbxTe3, which may serve as a versatile control mechanism. Our proposed approach may serve as a general framework for identifying and characterizing non-linear topological materials in actual scenarios. The unique predictions made about Ta1-xNbxTe3, such as the square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal phase, the 3D "Fermi pocket" structure, the C-shapped Fermi arc trajectories along the M-K-M' trajectory in the reciprocal space, the influence of the Te atomic layer distortion on the square-root higher-order Weyl behavior, the electric field and strain induced changes to the square-root higher-order Weyl behavior, suggest that this material may serve as an ideal model to test the theoretical framework developed in this study. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is achieved by using a Tikhonov-like method and the cost function includes the residual of the numerical solution with respect to the original equation, the boundary data, and the square of the normal component of the electric field on the incomplete boundary segment. A finite element method is employed to solve the resulting optimization problem. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through numerical examples, where the accuracy of the reconstruction is assessed against increasing inequality constraints, using synthetic data, and real-world data from a experiment where a conductive object was located inside a rectangular room. The results show that this method yields reliable solutions when the number of incomplete boundary points is relatively small, but runs into issues as this number increases. The solution algorithm is sensitive to the initial guess, which can negatively impact the quality of the reconstruction. The accuracy of the reconstruction also depends heavily on the spatial and temporal resolution of the numerical solution, as well as the time step and mesh size used in the simulation, where increasing these parameters beyond certain limits can significantly lower the reconstruction accuracy. The results presented in this study were obtained using a Lagrange multiplier method and the finite element method, but the approach can be applied to other numerical solutions of the time-varying Maxwell equations. The study also discusses some theoretical aspects of the method, such as the stability and convergence of the solution, as well as the relationship between the regularization parameter and the number of incomplete boundary points, but these issues remain areas of ongoing research. The study concludes by analyzing some computational complexity aspects of the method, which can be improved further, and presenting some ideas for future research, such as extending the method to nonlinear equations and improving the algorithm to reduce the sensitivity to the initial guess. The numerical solution and associated MATLAB code are provided in the online appendices. The Tikhonov method discussed in this study shares some commonalities with the quasi-reversibility method, which is also used to solve a data completion problem for the Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, but the two methods have distinct differences, the quasi-reversibility method being a more general term for a class of methods that aim to resolve the problem by using a suitable numerical solution to the original equation, without the need for the boundary data, without delving into the specifics of the underlying physical principles, the purpose of which is to ensure the smoothness of the solution, which in turn ensures the smoothness

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Collection (FSC) issue, a new problem that arises in interconnecting distributed knowledge bases, specifically in a federated setting. We envision a scenario where different data sources, represented as description logics ontologies, are connected through a query exchange, with sources acting either passively by storing data or actively by contributing data and answering queries. The FSC task aims to determine which active sources should contribute their data and which should answer queries to achieve a desired target ontology. We establish the connection between FSC and the inverse query learning problem, and show that solving FSC is equivalent to solving an inverse learning problem for the active sources. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FSC can be solved by employing an inverse learning approach, and provide a protocol for a federated setting. Additionally, we tackle the problem of sources that contribute both data and answer queries, and provide a solution by employing an automatic reasoning-based method. Lastly, we present an implementation of FSC and evaluate its performance on real-world data. The proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy, while also handling complex situations efficiently. The proposed solution in the experimental evaluation demonstrates the benefits of FSC in a variety of scenarios. The code for the proposed solution as well as data used in the experimental evaluation are available online. The FSC issue and the related solutions can be applied in various scenarios, including but not limited to scenario where there are multiple cancer types and sub-types, and a patient may have multiple conditions. We analyze the effect of extending the rational numbers to quartic fields within the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$ on the rank of an elliptic curve. Previously established results for rank growth hold in the non-diagonal case, where the quartic field's minimal polynomial contains no repeated roots. In the diagonal case, we find that the rank increases by 3 when the discriminant of the quadratic subfields is square-free, assuming a specific version of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. If the quadratic subfields have a common discriminant, the rank instead increases by 6. These findings arise from a direct computation of the rank growth component within the ideal group and the determination of 2-torsion points within the quartic extension. The main contribution also includes a proof that the rank growth is driven solely by the rank growth component, and a discussion on the relation between the 2-torsion points and the Shaferevich-Weil group. The key result for the diagonal case also holds when considering a family of elliptic curves over the quartic extensions, allowing us to demonstrate that a particular version of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture is valid for a specific family of elliptic curves. The research presented here is a combination of previous works by other authors and the results of the current study, which include the key findings for the rank growth in the diagonal case and the discussion on the relation between the 2-torsion points and the Shaferevich-Weil group. The main contribution of the current research is the analysis of the rank increase in the diagonal case, which has not been studied before. This study highlights the potential of integrated quantum elements, combining multiple materials, to facilitate efficient device characterization and increase coherence times. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is a contribution to the EUROVELENS project.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Nonetheless, SN~2020jfo's explosive energy and iron group element abundances fell within the normal Type II range. Semi-analytical modelling predicted an initial mass loss of less than 10 solar masses for SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is consistent with the absence of prominent interstellar absorption features in its spectrum. The detection of X-rays in wide-field observations poses a challenge due to the extensive field of view required and the limited angular resolution needed for signal identification. Conventional optical arrangements, relying on mirror systems for focusing X-rays, face limitations in monitoring extended sources and multiple targets simultaneously. A novel concept, inspired by the lobster's unique eyes that allow wide-field vision and high-resolution sight in specific directions, proposes an innovative optical design where multiple narrow-beam detectors are pointed towards a vast, scattered X-ray field. This "lobster-eye" design can be applied to experimental setups where multiple sources or scattered particles are monitored and could significantly enhance the capability for wide-field X-ray monitoring in various applications. The optimization of this design also presents an intriguing mathematical problem that can be resolved using available algorithms. The potential uses of this design are not restricted to X-rays, as it can be adapted for the detection of other forms of electromagnetic radiation. The lobster-eye concept can be implemented using a range of materials, including reflective materials, and the design is versatile enough to incorporate moving parts that could be achieved with a combination of mechanical and electromagnetic means. The current paper focuses on a simple, two-branch lobster-eye design; however, the concept can be expanded to more complex arrangements with multiple branches. The detection capabilities of a two-branch lobster-eye design have been evaluated through simulations of various scenarios, including the observation of X-ray binaries, supernovae remnantsc, and neutron star glitches. The results show that this design can effectively detect targets even with a large angle scattering, due to the focused beam in the particular direction, while simultaneously observing a wide field of the sky. The current paper also presents an approach to optimize the arrangement of the lobster-eye optics, as well as a calculation of the detection efficiency that can be used for other configurations of this design. The potential of this unique optical arrangement in combining high-resolution and wide-field vision makes it an highly effective tool in various astronomical observations. The current paper is organized as follows: the theoretical background and the design of the lobster-eye optics are discussed in section 2; the simulation scenarios are presented in section 3; the detection efficiency calculation is explained in section 4; the optimization of the arrangement is discussed in section 5; and the conclusions are summarized in section 6. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time identification required for multi-messenger astronomy. We detail a deep learning platform developed in-house, entitled WaveNet, and highlight the challenges faced and potential improvements. Given the expected rate of detections for future LIGO-like detectors, we also explore methods to enhance the network's efficiency. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the promising potential of deep learning in identifying signals from real LIGO data, and provides a crucial foundation for developing a low-latency detection system for real-time multi-messenger astronomy. Given its open-source nature, the WaveNet code is available for download upon request. Given the limited number of neutron star and binary neutron star mergers detected, we also explore a'soft' classification approach, which assigns a probability to each event based on its match to a trained model. Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar territories poses a significant challenge for mobile robots, citing trade-offs between exploration and safety. To address this issue, we present an innovative method for the controller layers of a navigation system to incorporate real-time sonar sensors. Unlike prior approaches that utilized sonar data in static maps, our proposal integrates sonar scans with the world map in real time, enabling the system to assess the environment and select the most suitable action instantly. We have tested and evaluated our sonar-based method against a marker-based localization approach and found that it offers a superior performance in uncertain environments. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that our method surpasses the conventional approach in areas with dynamic obstacles and provides a more expansive coverage in narrower areas. The results have been derived from simulations and actual experiments conducted in controlled and open settings. The findings have been presented in the form of graphs and compared to the existing methods, cementing our proposal as a superior solution for the navigation system in question. Our method has been implemented using the C++ programming language and the Player/Stage simulation platform, and the data obtained has been plotted using the R programming language. The outcome of this research can be utilized in various applications, including the development of autonomous guided vehicles, in addition to navigating public areas and intricate industrial settings. The sonar-based method we have presented is versatile and can be integrated with various controller layers of navigation systems, thereby providing a valuable contribution to the robotics community. The proposal consists of five sections: introduction, sonar sensor integration, evaluation, discussion, and conclusion. The study has been funded by the University of Malaya and the Ministry of Higher Education of Malaysia, and the development of the sonar-based method has been performed by a single researcher. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, as well as paths forward for future research in the field. We also present a notable incidence of false news that demonstrates the limitations of current approaches and the challenges it poses. This research was conducted in collaboration with a television news company, and we discuss a related application called News Compact, a system that employs machine learning for automatic text summarization to generate more concise versions of news articles, enabling faster reading and more efficient fact-checking. This system as well as our detection method have been deployed on the television company's website and are available at https://www.factbuzz.com/news/what-happened. We also provide the code for both projects on GitHub at https://github.com/FactBuzz/CMTR_BERT.

When analyzing data that contains a dependent direction, traditional Principal Component Analysis (PCA) may fail to effectively capture the underlying structure. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring methods that take into account the rotationally invariant property of their data. In this context, the aim of Rotationally Invariant $\ell_1$-PCA (RI-PCA) is to identify a direction that maximizes the absolute distance between data points located on one side of the hyperplane defined by this direction compared to those on the other side. The problem of finding this direction is challenging because it involves solving a challenging nonconvex problem with two distinct optimal solutions, namely the rotationally invariant version and the original PCA problem. Building on the previous work, this paper develops a linearly convergent, first-order algorithm that can solve the RI-PCA problem in an efficient manner. Additionally, the results of simulated data sets and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this paper's method. In particular, the paper finds that RI-PCA algorithm outperforms traditional PCA and $\ell_1$-PCA in terms of recovery rate and accuracy in scenarios involving dependent directions. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the review and revision of semantic annotations for a dataset containing emotion-related questions. To accomplish this, we develop a method that combines human inspectors, BERT, and rule-based systems to identify potential annotation errors and suggest targeted corrections. Furthermore, we establish that using BERT to review annotations for the same category yields a 72% reduction in misclassification error. The resulting annotated dataset and annotation correction method serve as valuable tools for the study of emotion-related questions. High-performance computing on SIMD devices like GPUs requires object-based programming, which can be challenging due to limited register resources and inefficient memory usage. Despite the efficiency of stack-based memory allocation, it hasn't been widely used on GPUs because existing implementations fail to utilize full parallelism when allocating memory. In response, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator that uses a stack-based approach and incorporates multiple threads to expedite memory fragmentation repair, block allocation, and caching. By minimizing memory accesses and maximizing register utilization, DynaSOAr significantly boosts performance on complex simulations like molecular dynamics from 2 to 5 times and reduces memory allocation latency by employing a novel binary search technique. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's efficiency in minimizing memory wastes and tightening object sizing leads to an average 19% decrease in execution speed when compared to other efficient memory allocators. When applying it to general GPU programs, DynaSOAr yields an average performance boost of 25% along with improved memory usage. The DynaSOAr allocator is suited for a variety of applications and delivers superior outcomes with popular simulations like Lattice Boltzmann Methods, Fluid Dynamics, and Monte Carlo Methods. The source code for DynaSOAr is now available as an open-source project on GitHub along with evaluation results for other simulations and applications.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, creating polarized positrons using this method on solid targets has been challenging due to the random polarization directions of positrons. A theoretical study suggests that positrons emitted perpendicular to a mirror-like surface made of thin metal films displayed polarized densities that could be quite high, potentially reaching 100% with a polarization angle of 45 degrees, depending on the incident laser intensity and the dielectric properties of the film. Conversely, the same parameters under a strong magnetic field revealed the potential for extremely high polarized densities of up to 10 times that of solid sources, achieved with a polarization angle of 20 degrees for specific film targets. Notably, the degree of polarization is influenced by the standing wave pattern of the electric field within the film, and the effectiveness of polarization is significantly enhanced when the film thickness aligns with half the wavelength of the electric field, which is typically in the range of tens to hundreds of nanometers. The predicted results agree with experimental findings of highly polarized positrons produced through interactions with thin film targets in the context of strong-field QED, and the theoretical model provides insights into the relationship between the degree of polarization and target characteristics, which could be crucial for optimizing sources of polarized particles. The predicted phenomenon of extremely high density polarized positrons emitted perpendicular to the surface of the film, coupled with the potential for further polarization enhancement via the application of a strong magnetic field, makes thin film targets particularly attractive for producing highly polarized positrons, specifically in the realm of strong-field QED. The potential for realizing dense polarized positrons in experiments using solid-state targets, which have been extensively developed, provides a promising pathway for creating sources of polarized particles. The theoretical model underlying these findings suggests that the density and polarization angle of the emitted positrons can be regulated by adjusting the laser intensity, the dielectric properties of the target, and the film thickness, which could be achieved through a combination of established technological means, and is therefore a realistic and feasible goal for immediate experimental verification. The predicted effects of dense polarized positrons emitted from thin film targets also offer potential applications in the study of strong-field quantum electrodynamics and the regularization of positron sources, which could be used in a variety of medical, industrial, and scientific contexts, including particle accelerator research, cancer treatment using particle therapy, and material characterization using positron annihilation spectroscopy. This research develops a 4-bit CMOS temperature detector employing a single-threshold inverting amplifier, providing the benefit of reduced power consumption and memory usage. The temperature detector comprises two separate detection sections, each utilizing a different threshold voltage to enhance accuracy and allow for self-calibration. The temperature range is divided into three sections, each mapped to a 4-bit binary code based on the temperature detection points (TDPs). A novel TDP extraction method was devised, incorporating process variations and production testing. The temperature is calculated by converting the TDP codes to temperature values using a lookup table. The temperature detector was designed to operate in a 65nm CMOS process, featuring a small footprint of 13.5μm x 13.5μm per detection section. Experimental results show that the temperature detector can accurately determine temperatures between 0.6V and 1.8V power supplies, covering a range of -70°C to 85°C with a resolution of 0.24°C and a power consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion. The design's low power consumption, small area, and limited memory usage make it suitable for low-power wireless communication applications, temperature-sensitive memory, and look-up tables in digital temperature detectors. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, a phenomenon supported by core mass function data.  Furthermore, the mean mass of protostellar cores exceeds the mean mass of the surrounding gas and dust within a 2 pc^2 area.  These findings suggest that mass accumulation occurs at the core's center rather than its periphery.  In fact, a comparison of the mass distribution within cores to the surrounding environment reveals that the mass structure is inversely applied, indicating that cores are actually less dense than their surrounding environment.  This density discrepancy holds the potential to be a critical factor in regulating the core's collapse into a massive star, demonstrating that only the most massive cores with a low internal density will proceed with massive star formation.  A comparison with the known outcomes of these cores also confirms this hypothesis, as only the most massive cores with low internal density have formed massive stars.  In point of fact, the threshold for this density limit appears to be approximately 10^3 times higher than the density required for their own collapse, suggesting that cores have expanded as a result of some form of thermal energy release, most likely from the formation of low-mass stars, and that this core expansion is necessary for massive star formation to occur.  This hypothesis is further supported by the presence of both very low mass and massive star formation within the Dragon cloud, as well as the phenomenon of massive star formation that is currently inactive, indicating that this process is a gradual one that takes place over a long period of time.  Consequently, a plot of density versus mass provides a predictive model for the outcomes of these cores, offering valuable insights into the complex relationships between the physical properties of cores and their subsequent star formation outcomes.  This study was conducted using a comprehensive database of cores and star formation outcomes within the Dragon cloud, as well as a similar infrared dark cloud known as the Colombe umbra. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by a rough surface's texture, which can be hazardous for safety in various contexts such as waterways, surface skidding, and gas and oil extraction. To address this issue, research focuses on identifying effective texture patterns to minimize friction and associated problems. Previously, studies have demonstrated that anisotropic crystal formations in granular materials and two-dimensional cell patterns in liquid crystals exhibit optimal orientations that minimize friction. In contrast, this current study investigates the optimal texture patterns in liquid foams for minimizing friction. Due to the dynamic and highly unstable nature of foam crystals, direct measurement is challenging, thus we rely on theoretical approaches to analyze our findings. Specifically, we examined the geometry of foam crystals in two-scenario applications: surface textures and interface foams. In both cases, the orientation of the macroscopic crystal pattern influences the flow resistance significantly. Furthermore, we determine the most resistant and stable orientations of these patterns, which can be critical in preventing unsafe surface flow and improving the efficiency of gas and oil extraction. Moreover, our research reveals that circular ring textures exhibit high resistance compared to other patterns, which could be an interesting feature in its own right. Overall, our study on texture-induced friction in liquid foams highlights potential solutions for various industrial and everyday contexts. Lastly, we believe that this research can be extended to other complex non-Newtonian liquids beyond liquid foams.

In neural machine translation, generating text can be seen as a sequential process, one word at a time. Current approaches translate words simultaneously, without considering the effect of subsequent words. This technique, known as neural machine translation, utilizes encoder and decoder hidden states, without accounting for the upcoming context. We propose the look-ahead focus method, which determines a distinct initial hidden state for the decoder, based on the target sequence, to account for the context of subsequent words. We believe this technique enables the decoder to consider the upcoming context, although it doesn't actually see the context during the translation process. We hypothesize that during the initial stages of generation, the decoder's state should be influenced by the context of the remaining words, as it decides on earlier words. We validate this hypothesis by implementing the look-ahead focus method, which outperforms standard neural machine translation techniques. We achieve the best results when the proposed method is combined with conventional neural machine translation, using sentence ordering and different initial hidden states. We also analyze the proposed method's effectiveness in various translation scenarios. The code for the look-ahead focus method is available at https://github.com/ghulam-saqib/Neural-Machine-Translation. The proposed method also enables the model to focus on important words, even if they are distant, which is particularly effective when the vocabulary is vast. The proposed approach offers several benefits, including the simplicity of its implementation and the lack of additional parameters, which makes it suitable for integration with existing neural machine translation techniques. Our primary goal is to examine the convergence of $M^n_t$ as it relates to the product of two independent random variables, $K_t$ and $L_t$, where $K_t$ represents the maximum of $M^n_t$ across all intervals up to time $t$, and $L_t$ represents the linear combination of $M^n_t$ within those same intervals. Our main conclusion is that both $K_t$ and $L_t$ converge to the same constant value $c$ as $n$ approaches infinity, and this convergence occurs at a rate that is directly proportional to the square root of $n$. Our research also provides two novel corollaries that pertain to the random walk $X^n_t$ itself. Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our aim is to demonstrate that imperative algorithms are, in fact, a representation of universal quantified proofs, which can be derived from the original specifications that defined their validity. This task can be seen as a mapping between the original data and a more concise representation, effectively defining a clustering of the data. The problem has been extensively studied for static data sets across various metrics, however, the focus shifts to the implementation of the algorithm on dynamic data sets, where frequent additions and deletions of data points occur. We introduce a novel type of stochastic chase-evasion games on structured objects, incorporating separate hierarchical representations that divide the space into distinct entities. A key feature of these games is the presence of a pervasive agent that pursues an evader across these structured elements, whereas the manager agent, which has access to local information, needs to make decisions for a specific region. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on two-player games, we establish the possibility of collaborative gameplay between the pervasive agent and region managers to address large-scale challenges. To facilitate this collaboration, we develop an efficient hierarchical strategy using a decomposition that breaks down the space into simpler subspaces, allowing for feasible computation. Furthermore, we establish that hierarchical policies can lead to near-optimal outcomes in extensive domains. To illustrate the versatility of our model, we apply it to a specific case study, a stochastic hierarchical chase-evasion game on the web, for which we derive a hierarchical decomposition and show that our approach yields a superior outcome compared to a non-hierarchical model. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to catastrophic interference. To overcome this issue, we
demonstrate that isolating sub-networks for each task, while keeping parameters
shared only at a modular level, yields a substantial improvement in performance.
We show that this approach outperforms the standard multi-task learning method
and that the advantages increase as the number of diverse tasks grows. Moreover
alongside multi-initialization reinforcement learning challenges, our approach
also demonstrates superior performance in random mask experiments and shows that
it adheres to established scalability characteristics. Our code has been made publicly
available at: https://github.com/ghul131/multitask-dynamics-networks.

The model we introduced is scalable, enabling the exploration of complex states such as the mentioned linear order's fragmentation and the effects of introducing "liars" or "logicians". In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on capturing the variety of possible outcomes - effectively recovering the underlying probability distribution. This research involves developing a new algorithm to generate a regularized posterior density estimate via Conditional Regularized GANs. By combining the strengths of regularized and conditional GANs, we obtain a superior density estimate with a lower reconstruction cost compared to conventional methods, while producing high-quality samples that closely match the ground truth, as evaluated in experiments conducted on multiple datasets. The proposed algorithm can be used as a base for various inversion solutions or employed simply to enhance density estimation and image sampling. The associated code is available for public use.

This research paper examines a specific type of symmetry called invariant surfaces that can exist within certain dynamical systems. These surfaces possess a particular property where their composition with the system results in the surface itself being recognizable from the original system. We have successfully proved that beyond a specific fractionality threshold, certain hyperbolic dynamical systems fail to support these invariant surfaces. This achievement is made possible by introducing a new concept related to the system's fractionality, called the local fractionality, which helps bridge the gap between the Bondissimilarity concept and the fractionality property. Furthermore, our findings also demonstrate that above this defined threshold, even the surface itself cannot remain stable. This discovery also extends to a broader context, where it applies to partial differential equations and certain fractional order nonlinear systems. Additionally, we have identified specific conditions under which these results can be applied, including those related to the system's fractionality and the dimension of the system's state. These conditions vary depending on whether the system in question is of parabolic or elliptic nature. Our existing nonexistence results for invariant surfaces are also supported by numerical simulations presented in a special section called the appendix. The pulsar B1133+16, located at a sky position of 11.76 ddeg, exhibits significant variability in its width, potentially reflecting interactions with local matter. Pulsar scintillation measurements can vary regionally, depending on the interstellar medium, and have been studied over a wide range of frequencies and sky areas by analyzing pulsar data. This paper utilizes pulsar scintillation data from archival observations of the pulsar B1133+16, spanning frequencies and sky positions, to investigate the regional characteristics of the interstellar medium. Evaluating the width of the pulse profile over time at both 1.4 and 3.2 ddeg sky areas revealed similar variability patterns, indicating that the primary factor affecting pulse profile width is the distribution of ionized matter within the line of sight rather than the specific sky area. Additionally, analyzing the characteristics of scintillation bandwidth at both 1.4 and 3.2 ddeg sky areas showed that the bandwidth is comparable, with a mean frequency bandwidth of approximately 3.5 MHz for both areas. Furthermore, evaluating the properties of the interstellar medium within the line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16, with a distance estimated to be greater than 500 pc, showed that the properties of the interstellar medium in this region are comparable to those found in other lines of sight to the Galactic plane. Lastly, interpreting the results within the broader context of the surrounding interstellar medium, including the molecular cloud associated with the pulsar and the nearby HII region, may provide insights into the dynamics of the matter interacting with the pulsar. Nevertheless, the data at hand do not sufficiently detail the spatial distribution of the associated matter to draw such inferences with confidence. Nevertheless, analyzing the properties of the pulse profile width and scintillation bandwidth at both 1.4 and 3.2 ddeg sky areas within the line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16 provides a specific and useful case study of the regional characteristics of the interstellar medium. Such knowledge can be applied to other pulsars, enabling a broader understanding of the interstellar medium and its impact on pulsar searches and astrophysical/signal processing investigations. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through an innovative pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation by utilizing a deeply cascaded autoregressive architecture, yet its limited pitch control results from converted learned features instead of direct pitch signals being incorporated. To address this constraint, we propose a pitch-dependent expanded convolutional network where each stage draws from a combination of general and task-specific models. General models are shared across stages and facilitate global waveform understanding, while task-specific models are stage-independent and allow for local waveform analysis. The proposed network allows for direct incorporation of pitch signals through vector concatenation, thereby enhancing the limited pitch control of WN. Experimental evaluations on the LJSpeech and VCTK datasets demonstrate the improved pitch control of QPNet compared to WN, along with its increased computational requirements. To further accommodate longer periodic signals, we introduced a rolling prediction framework for QPNet, leading to a trade-off between pitch control and computational load. Our primary goal in this research is to demonstrate the challenging nature of a visual noise localization task for current state-of-the-art computer vision models. To achieve this, we design a novel dataset called LVD (Local Visual Noise Dataset) to accurately measure the ability of models in distinguishing small objects from background noise. Our findings suggest that models perform poorly at both simple and complex noise object recognition tasks, and that this difficulty is not due to a lack of training data, but rather a fundamental limitation of the models. To further explore this insight, we create a sequential noise localization task where models must first identify the location of a noise object before classifying it, and our results show that models struggle significantly with this task. To demonstrate that this challenge is specific to the current generation of models, we train a robust convolutional neural network that excels at this task. Our research contributes a valuable tool for evaluating computer vision models and our results have significant implications for the development of robust vision models. Our code and data are available for public use at https://github.com/chenwen1533/LVD. Our findings have been published in our paper Localizing Visual Noises the Hard Way, which was presented at the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2023). The paper can be found at: https://openaccess.eurocon2023.org/index.php/home?option=article&articleid=202301331. The LVD dataset is an extension of the noise object recognition dataset proposed by Xiong et al. in their paper Simple Neural Network for Noise Object Recognition, which was presented at the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2020). The code for the robust convolutional neural network can be found at: https://github.com/chenwen1533/RCNN. Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by their application in representing complex and dynamic graphs, which are commonplace in various real-world scenarios. As a result, there's an increasing need to explore GNN's potential in analyzing relationships that are optimized, such as in link prediction tasks. Nevertheless, a significant issue in GNN training involves overcoming the hyperparameter obstacles, which can be compounded by the scarcity of abundant node attribute data, a common challenge in various real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel method called Lorentzian GNN, which leverages the principles of Lorentzian space to create a new, alternative framework for comparing nodes, along with a novel optimization objective that can handle restricted access to node attribute data, namely in link prediction tasks. In our experiments, Lorentzian GNN demonstrated consistently superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, with compound pathways and protein-protein interaction networks examples showcasing the versatility of our approach. The associated code is available at https://github.com/Lingeng/Lorentzian-GNN.

data on college students. We also demonstrate that our model's impulse control

Using advanced neural styling tools for photo editing, we investigate the potential risks they pose in misleading medical professionals with incorrectly labeled patient data. Our study utilizes a dataset for lung pathologia by combining the CheXpert images with artistic styles, and investigates how neural editors affect the accuracy of AI models. Our findings show that even when these tools are used to create realistic modifications, they can still mislead the models to the same extent as more extreme manipulations, such as exchanging patient profiles. We believe that our research highlights the importance of relying on primary clinical sources for patient data, and that photo editing tools are not a suitable alternative for scaling up labeled datasets. We also offer recommendations for further improving the integrity of future datasets. Our work includes an open source code for editing CheXpert images and measuring the effectiveness of neural styling tools to manipulate medical models. We hope that our study and code will contribute to the development of more robust and illness-aware medical models. If used appropriately, such models can ensure that medical AI systems remain reliable and cannot be deceived by fabricated patient data. Our study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board at Stanford University. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/ghrua/surgical-stylings. We have also uploaded the dataset we created to the CheXpert website. We have presented our findings at the medical AI conferences ICSER and MEDI. We have further discussed the risks and potential solutions associated with photo editing on the blog https://med.ai/. We have included an appendix that addresses concerns related to quality and artificial synthesis. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and in-depth examination, featuring a user-friendly interface that allows users to easily manage and visualize complex data sets consisting of multiple vectors across different dimensions. The tool offers various visualization options for high-dimensional data, including projections, trajectories defined by linear differential equations, and weighted graph representations. Furthermore, ViDaExpert incorporates an integrated framework for methodological developments in nonlinear dimension reduction and trajectory analysis in high-dimensional data contexts. The application is suitable for general-purpose use and is particularly useful for methodological researchers in statistics and computer science. The code for ViDaExpert is available on GitHub under the MIT license. The application is available for use on Windows, macOS, and Linux operating systems. The name ViDaExpert is derived from Vectorial Data Expert. The previous version of this tool was known as ViDaVisualizer. The application was originally developed as part of the PhD studies at the University of Lyon. The development of ViDaExpert was facilitated by the ANR JCJC Ccrowd project.
